articles.title_orig: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.title_zh: From Rifle to the world: DM Vans surpasses 800-van mark
articles.content_orig:
psullivan@postindependent.com
DM Vans builds its camper vans today in a state-of-the-art, 20,000-square-foot facility in Rifle.
The company has come a long way from the original production site: the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
DM Vans co-founder Matt Fesler built this first van out of necessity.
“I wanted something I could travel through the mountains with, bring my skis, bring my bikes, bring my golf clubs, and stay in comfortably,” Fesler said. “At the time, there really wasn’t something out there on the market that fit what I was looking for within my budget.”
Felser was a teacher at Vail Mountain School at the time and needed a vehicle that could serve as a portable base camp for his adventures.
With the help of YouTube tutorials and some friends, the first Dave and Matt, or DM, van came to fruition in the Vail Mountain School parking lot.
Fesler and his friend, and eventual DM Vans co-founder, Dave Ramsay, soon realized that they had done more than build the vehicle that Fesler was looking for.
The pair “realized that (they) had something, something that was simple, reliable, easier to use than what was on the market, and obviously more affordable,” Fesler said.
After living in that first van for nine months, which he “loved to death,” Fesler got the itch to build more.
“So I sold that first one, used that to build two, sold two, built four, sold four, built eight, and yeah, here we are, eight years later, and 800 vans,” Fesler said.
The 800 Ram ProMaster vans which DM vans transformed into parking-spot-sized homes are now spread across 48 states, and the company shows no signs of slowing down.
Although the 30-person team, and sheer scale of the operation are a far cry from the early days of DM Vans, some things have stayed the same.
“We’ve used the tagline ‘everything you need, nothing you don’t’ from day one,” Fesler said. “That was kind of how I wanted to approach it in terms of something that was simple and reliable that would get me from A to B comfortably and allow me to stay there and pursue my passions, and it is amazing how that design philosophy has stayed from day one through now.”
That does not mean DM Vans has shied away from technological advances to improve their product, however.
With smaller, lighter and more powerful lithium batteries on the market, DM Vans can run heating, air conditioning, running water, refrigeration and other appliances off relatively small power supply.
Using a computer numerical control, or CNC, machine, the company can cut out wooden parts with precision and ease.
DM Vans hopes to build 145 vans in the coming year.
The combination of the “van-life” boom and navigating the coronavirus pandemic gave the pair their fair share of obstacles to navigate.
“Dave (Ramsay) and I joke a lot that we very much had the best MBA program you could possibly go on in our eight-year journey here of the highest of highs, lowest of lows, but are really excited for the stability that we now have as a business, the incredible employees we have in Rifle and around Colorado,” Fesler said.
After eight years of successful business and growth, Fesler is proud of how far the company has come.
“The numbers of businesses that go out of business after five years are staggering, right? To make it to 10 is truly something that would be that peak moment for us, and so just being here doing something that we love is the thing that makes me the most proud,” Fesler said.

An Iranian cleric warned Friday that oil tankers and airports across the region could face disruption if Iran 's oil exports or air travel are cut off, according to Iran International.
Hossein Hosseini Karnami, the Friday prayer leader in Sari, tied Iran's fate to that of its neighbors during a sermon.
"If our airport is to be closed, no airport in the region will remain open, and if our oil is not exported, no oil tanker will pass through the Persian Gulf," Karnami said, according to the outlet.
He also said "resistance and the soldiers of this land" would help determine whether the Strait of Hormuz remained open or closed.
The remarks came the same day the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported that a tanker traveling through the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile, resulting in a small fire and blackout. No casualties were reported.
Iran International did not report that Karnami was announcing an official policy of Iran's government or military.
President Donald Trump said Friday that he expects the war with Iran to end "very soon" and predicted oil prices will fall sharply once the conflict is over.
Speaking at a midterm campaign rally in Mobile, Alabama, Trump pointed to Iran's economic troubles and claimed the country is experiencing roughly 310% inflation.
"Their economy is down the tubes. They have one thing they really do have. It's called inflation. They have about 310% inflation. And we'll see what happens," Trump said.
"But as soon as we it's going to end very soon, probably right after the election. But as soon as it does end, oil prices will come tumbling down."
Trump later returned to the timeline, saying the war would end "one way or the other" and again suggesting a resolution could come shortly after the midterm elections.
"That war is going to be over soon. One way or the other, one way or the other. It's going to end very soon and probably right after the midterms," Trump said.
Trump also said oil prices could ultimately fall below the levels seen during his first term once the conflict ends.
A crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile off the coast of Oman on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said.
The vessel's master reported that the projectile hit the port side of the tanker about four nautical miles east of Oman, according to UKMTO.
All crew members were reported safe, and there was no reported environmental impact as of Friday evening.
Authorities are investigating the incident, while UKMTO advised vessels traveling through the area to exercise caution and report suspicious activity.
The incident comes amid heightened threats to commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz .
U.S. Central Command released new imagery Friday showing an Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle conducting operations over the Middle East as Washington bolsters its military presence in the region.
The fighter jet was photographed receiving fuel from a KC-135 Stratotanker during a patrol, according to CENTCOM.
The imagery comes as the Pentagon sends additional forces to the Middle East. U.S. officials confirmed to Fox News on Thursday that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are headed to the region.
The deployments are expected to add about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the U.S. presence in the Middle East.
The G7 will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from emergency reserves in an effort to stabilize energy supplies as the Iran war pushes prices higher, according to Reuters.
The four-month release will begin immediately, with a substantial amount of diesel expected to enter the market during the first 20 days, according to a joint statement.
President Donald Trump announced Friday that Europe had agreed to release a "massive" amount of diesel and said the U.S. would not restrict its own diesel exports.
"Europe has a lot of diesel, and they're going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we. And we're not going to be doing the export ban," Trump said.
The move comes as disruptions from the Iran war have strained energy markets and increased Europe's reliance on U.S. diesel.
Iran has floated political engagement with Yemen's Houthis as an alternative to military action following attacks by the group, Pakistan's foreign minister said Friday, according to Iran International.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the idea emerged during discussions with Tehran and is not a formal proposal.
"There is no written, solid offer. It is brainstorming between two foreign ministers," Dar said.
The proposal is expected to be discussed next week when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey hold an emergency meeting in Riyadh under their Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.
Dar also said Iranian officials had distanced Tehran from the Houthis and Iraqi militias and indicated they wanted the situation resolved.
The FlyDubai co-pilot accused of stabbing the captain of a passenger jet mid-flight and nearly causing a catastrophic crash was grounded by Oman Air in 2024 after the airline discovered he had been visiting radical Islamic websites, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Authorities believe the co-pilot moved to Dubai later that same year, according to the source, who also told Fox News the co-pilot spent a significant part of his life outside Oman, including with his mother, who is from Syria.
According to the source, FlyDubai did not check with Oman Air about the co-pilot before hiring him.
The new details come as The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter, that the Omani national had previously been banned from flying over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views before later being hired by FlyDubai. The newspaper reported it was unclear whether Omani officials shared those concerns with other countries or airlines.
Fox News has not independently verified the reason the co-pilot was grounded by Oman Air.
This is an excerpt of an article from Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller and John Roberts
President Donald Trump 's counterterrorism chief said the administration's standoff with Iran will "imminently be resolved," while offering no details about what could come next.
Sebastian Gorka, deputy assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council, made the comment in an interview with The Jerusalem Post.
Gorka said Trump's demands regarding Iran's nuclear program, support for proxies and activities in the region have not changed.
"Nothing has changed with regard to the president," Gorka said. "Now the decision lies with the mullah in Iran."
Gorka did not explain what he meant by "imminently" or indicate whether his remarks referred to military action, diplomacy or another potential development.
A senior United Arab Emirates official publicly characterized the suspected attack aboard a FlyDubai flight to Israel as terrorism for the first time Friday as investigators continued working to determine the alleged attacker's motive and whether he acted alone.
Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed, called the incident a "dangerous and potentially catastrophic act of terrorism" while praising pilot Smit Machchhar, according to The Times of Israel.
Authorities say Machchhar was stabbed by his Omani co-pilot before passengers and other pilots aboard the flight intervened. The aircraft, carrying around 180 passengers, made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said investigators are now examining whether someone directed the alleged attacker.
"We are clarifying right now if he was sent," Netanyahu said. "And whoever sent him will pay a heavy price."
No connection to Iran has been established. President Donald Trump said Thursday that Tehran may have been involved but said the investigation remained underway.

articles.title_orig: Hollister teen to compete for Team USA at 2026 World Skate Games
articles.title_zh: Hollister teen to compete for Team USA at 2026 World Skate Games
articles.content_orig:
Dominic Rosales, a 16-year-old goaltender from Hollister, has been selected to represent Team USA's junior inline hockey team at the 2026 World Skate Games in Asunción, Paraguay, marking the biggest tournament of his career.
"I just want to, like, take the most out of it, experience how South America is going to be, having to represent Team USA. Play with my friends, you know, I think that will be the most I want to take out of it. Obviously, winning a gold medal would be cool too," Rosales said.
A gold medal would be a fitting achievement for Rosales, who has already proven himself as one of the nation's elite young goaltenders.
Rosales grew up watching his father, Diego, play as a goalie, inspiring him to pursue the position himself. His passion for the sport started early, even leading him to dress up as a goalie for Halloween.
"Me and my buddy just MacGyvered that thing. We just got a bunch of tape, cardboard, and hard foam, and we made his own little set. He was super happy. After Halloween, he used it every single day outside. He was able to slide across in the living room, and he thought he was the next goalie, you know? And it worked," Diego said.
Diego has been instrumental in supporting his son's dream, working three jobs over the years to ensure Dominic could pursue his passion for hockey.
"I think the most rewarding things out of this, sure, I'll take another job, another shift, do extra jobs here and there. I think the fact that he loves the sport makes it so much worth it, right? And we can look past all the rest of it," Diego said.
As Rosales prepares to compete on the world stage, he carries the pride of his hometown with him.
"It fills me with pride because I know Hollister will have my back and support me. They've been supporting me with this journey. I think, definitely coming back, I'll have a lot of pride. I'm happy I'm able to represent Hollister, a small town," Rosales said.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike unconscious and on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, the woman who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee earlier this week, remains hospitalized in critical condition, her lawyers said in a new statement Friday.
She is unconscious, intubated and breathing through a ventilator. The death row inmate is also being treated for “significant injuries to both arms” sustained when two lethal injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her.
At one point, Pike said it felt like her arm was exploding, and she could be heard whimpering, according to her legal team.
“We are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” attorney Luke Ihnen said in a statement. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”
The state of Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death Wednesday night by lethal injection for a murder she committed when she was 18.
Pike, now 50, has been on death row for decades and would have been the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
NBC News earlier reported that there was no emergency medical oxygen in the execution room in case something went wrong. Medical professionals had to retrieve it from elsewhere.
Pike’s attorneys detailed her condition in a new emergency motion filed Friday asking the state to preserve all evidence from the failed execution attempt.
“In the words of one media witness: we have a lot of questions and the Department of Correction has a lot of answers that it needs to provide to the public about what happened here. We agree,” the motion reads.
In their filing, the lawyers described a painful and chaotic scene that unfolded in front of several witnesses, and that they said could have been prevented with the proper care and training.
Medical staff failed to follow basic protocol, like ensuring the needles used were fresh, functional and inserted properly, according to the motion. Further, the state did not heed Pike’s concerns prior to the procedure that preexisting medical conditions could make lethal injection difficult to complete, the motion says.
The motion accuses the department of corrections of “inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
The Tennessee Attorney General did not immediately return a request for comment on the new filing. A spokesperson for the state department of corrections said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
At a news conference Thursday, Stephen Ferrell and another of Pike’s attorneys, Randall Spivey, detailed how the execution attempt went wrong . Spivey, who was in the room, recalled Pike saying she was in pain, and like she felt like her arm was about to “explode.”
“It’s not supposed to be a cruel and an unusual execution,” criminologist Deborah Denno told NBC News. “The goal is to kill somebody, but to kill them within means or in a reasonable way, where there’s not going to be pain and suffering.”
According to Friday’s filing, the execution process lasted longer than two hours. Pike’s legal team filed emergency motions to halt the execution in multiple courts before the prison called an ambulance.
“Even then,” it continues, “attorneys for the State of Tennessee argued that TDOC had no obligation to render life-saving care to Ms. Pike.”
NBC News contributor Dr. Natalie Azar, a rheumatologist, said the pain Pike described could be attributed to pentobarbital flowing into her arm instead of straight into her veins. That would be painful with any medication, Azar said, but the specific properties of pentobarbital would make the experience exceptionally uncomfortable.
The scenario would also result in Pike being administered a less-than-lethal dose. It was enough to suppress her respiratory system but not enough to kill her, Azar explained. The question of how long Pike’s brain was deprived on oxygen will be central to her prognosis.
“There is no reversal of pentobarbital. There is no medicine or antidote,” she said. “You have to basically wait for the liver to metabolize the drug and get it out of your system.”
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder case. She and two other teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was sentenced to death. A number of last-minute legal efforts to stop Pike’s execution were unsuccessful.

articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
UPDATE: Apple has confirmed a problem affecting the AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max.
"We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls," Apple tells 9to5Mac . "We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”
The update is intended to prevent this from happening to other phones, 9to5Mac notes. If your iPhone has already lost service, you'll need to take it in to be replaced.
Original Story: Ever since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched last month, AT&T customers have complained about being unable to make calls, send texts, or use cellular data. According to MacRumors , the carrier acknowledged the issue in a text message to customers this week and recommended an immediate software upgrade to fix the issue.
“Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately,” reads AT&T’s message to customers.
Apple's iOS 27.0.1 began rolling out to iPhone users on Monday. The release notes mention patches for a Face ID bug and camera-zooming issues on iPhone 18 Pro models, as well as a fix for an unresponsive screen issue . No mention of AT&T issues, though.
Even after updating to iOS 27.0.1, cellular issues persist for some AT&T customers. "I cannot make or receive cellular phone calls on the brand-new phone I set up this morning," Lindsay Robertson, a writer and editor from Brooklyn, tells PCMag. "Nor can I make or receive them on my old phone. AT&T, you have ONE JOB!"
Robertson now plans to visit the AT&T store this weekend to re-activate her old phone before going to the Apple Store to get a replacement iPhone 18 Pro Max. "I will just have to pray that all that work fixed it," she says. "I spent over two hours talking to AT&T support this morning, with each minute becoming more infuriating."
It's unclear whether the issue lies with the carrier or the iPhone hardware. Neither Apple nor AT&T has explained the cause. If you want to try your luck, you can update your iPhone software by going to Settings > General > Software Update.
An AT&T spokesperson tells us that the Apple update should "address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts, and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones," adding, "Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right.”
On Apple’s Community forum , we spotted a few customers saying they visited an Apple Store, where staff ordered replacement units for them. Some have already received their new phones and say the AT&T connectivity issue has been resolved. Most of those comments were posted before Monday's iOS 27.0.1 update, so we have reached out to Apple for more details.
Editors' Note: This story was updated with comments from AT&T and Robertson.
Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

articles.title_orig: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.title_zh: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. economy created far fewer jobs than expected in September, pointing to a surprising soft spot in the labor market and broader economy.
Nonfarm payrolls rose a seasonally adjusted 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for job growth of 84,000 and an unemployment rate of 4.1%.
In addition to the weakness in September, the August jobs count was revised lower to reflect a gain of 133,000 while July switched from a gain to a loss as payrolls fell by 10,000. The revisions in total showed 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.
Market reaction was swift to the report, with traders interpreting the soft jobs numbers as good news as they likely further cemented the Federal Reserve staying put at its October meeting.
Stock futures rose sharply after the release while Treasury yields slumped after recently rising to levels not seen since the early part of the century. Market-implied odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at its Oct. 27-28 meeting jumped to 82.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a note.
"The payroll data surged in August, and we had expected the momentum to continue this month, given the historically low prints on jobless claims in recent weeks," he added. "However, it now appears that the August number was nothing more than a rebound from very weak hiring in June and July."
Fed officials more closely watch the unemployment rate than the headline payrolls numbers.
The household survey, which is used to calculate the jobless level, was considerably better than the establishment survey, which is used to derive the payrolls count.
Household employment rose by 406,000 for the month, while the labor force swelled by 485,000 and the participation rate, which counts those working or actively searching for a job as a share of the total labor force, increased 0.2 percentage point to 61.8%, its highest since May.
An alternative measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons, edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025.
The report comes with Federal Reserve officials weighing the state of the economy and how it should affect their next interest rate move.
Following statements in recent days from central bank policymakers, markets have recalibrated expectations and now expect the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee to hold off until December for its next hike. The FOMC raised benchmark rates a quarter percentage point in September.
Policymakers largely see inflation as a larger threat to the economy than the labor market, which had shown resilience in recent months. The data has painted a picture of a low-hire, low-fire economy, with weekly jobless claims low and one indicator showing layoffs at their lowest rate in four years.
Inflation, though, has held well above the Fed's 2% target. The most recent indicator of the central bank's preferred gauge showed core inflation at a 3% annual rate.
Wages, though, continued to show signs of disinflation.
Average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% in September, putting the 12-month gain at 3%, the lowest since May 2021. Wall Street had been looking for readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The average work week was unchanged at 34.6 hours.
"Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays."
However, Long described the labor market as "stable" and said she doesn't think the Fed will be dissuaded from hiking in December.
Most of the monthly job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers. Construction was up by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000.
Government employment fell by 17,000, while temporary help services saw a decline of 11,000, and information services lost 10,000 amid worries over the impact artificial intelligence may have on the jobs picture. Financial activities also saw a drop of 7,000 jobs.
The weak job growth comes despite signs of strength elsewhere.
On a macro level, economic growth has been strong.
Earlier this week, the Commerce Department revised its count of both first- and second-quarter gross domestic product growth, to 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively. The Atlanta Fed is tracking third-quarter GDP at 3.7%.

articles.title_orig: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue
articles.title_zh: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it has determined a new software glitch on some Boeing 737 Max aircraft isn't a flight-safety issue.
The determination paves the way to certification for the last model in the company's best-selling family of airplanes, the 737 Max 10, just as Boeing seeking to sell and deliver more aircraft after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing flagged the software issue, which could affect certain landing procedures, last month and the FAA on Monday said it was reviewing to determine if it poses a safety of flight issue.
"Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern," the FAA said. "The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
The FAA said on Friday that it will issue a special bulletin to airlines on how to recognize and respond to the issue if it arises.
The agency convened a review board on Friday to assess the issue. Participants included FAA experts on airframes, flight controls, propulsion, flight testing and others.
"As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue," the agency said.
U.S. airlines said they're not affected by the issue since they could revert to older versions of the software, but the problem raised questions about certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10, which Boeing and airlines expected to come in early fall.
The Max 10 is the largest in the family of airplanes and would be the last of the Max lineup to win government certification to fly. The FAA approved the Max 7 , the smallest in the Max family, in August.
Chief executives of 737 Max 10 customers, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, earlier this week brushed off concerns about the aircraft's certification delays.

articles.title_orig: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.title_zh: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.content_orig:
A nonprofit environmental group working with primates in Sebangau National Park says the dry peatlands can be a catalyst to more destruction.
(CN) â Since early August, wildfires have devastated the fragile rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, causing widespread toxic air across Indonesia. Itâs affected most communities in all parts of the region of Kalimantan, a part of the worldâs third largest island under Indonesiaâs governance.
The fires are fueled by shifting El NiÃ±o climate patterns, causing severe drought and extremely dry conditions in the islandâs peatlands, among the planetâs most effective carbon-capturing ecosystems and vital habitat for wildlife found nowhere else in the world.
Sebangau National Park in Central Kalimantan is home to an estimated 6,000 to 9,000 critically endangered Bornean orangutans, one of the islandâs largest populations. The nonprofit Borneo Nature Foundation said a fire crossed the park boundary for the first time in early September.
âOur teams pushed it back, and it was largely confined to sedge and open peat, but some reforestation sites are impacted,â Dr. Susan Cheyne, the Science Director for the Borneo Nature Foundation and the Vice Chair for the International Union for the Conservation of Nature special project group for small apes, said in an email to Courthouse News.
âOur priority is to keep fire out of the forest, because that protects every orangutan in it at once,â she said. Cheyne and her colleagues monitor and document conditions in Borneo, while volunteer firefighting crews work to keep fires out of orangutan habitat and nearby villages. Capturing and removing the apes is âa last resort,â Cheyne said.
Sebangau is also home to several of the worldâs rarest primates, including the largest known population of Bornean white-bearded gibbons, an ape Cheyne has studied for over 20 years.
Gibbons are known for their musical vocalizations, or âsongs.â Males sing alone in the morning before females join them in duets later in the day.
âDuring the 2006 fires I found that gibbons sang less often and sang shorter songs on smoky days. Their song is how they defend territory and keep pair bonds, so this matters,â said Cheyne. âA similar pattern has since been recorded in wild Bornean orangutans exposed to wildfire smoke.â
Gibbons rarely come to the ground, and fire survivors are often left in small, isolated forest patches with little food. Other primates, including red langurs and long-tailed and southern pig-tailed macaques, are found only in Southeast Asia, and each fire further reduces their numbers. Little is known about how fires affect nocturnal slow lorises and western tarsiers, Cheyne said.
The national park includes vast peat swamps, made of partly decomposed plant material accumulated over thousands of years. In parts of Sebangau, the peat dome reaches 12 meters deep.
Peatlands are naturally waterlogged, like giant sponges that do not burn. But in the 1990s and early 2000s, illegal loggers dug hundreds of canals to float timber out of the forest. Those canals continue draining the peat, causing it to dry out and become fuel.
âIn a long dry season like this one, a dried-out peat swamp is a tinderbox,â said Cheyne.
âWhat makes peat fires so hard to fight is that they burn downwards and sideways, not just across the surface. Fire smolders underground through the dry peat, sometimes for weeks, long after the flames above have gone out. These are sometimes called zombie fires.â
Peat fires are particularly dangerous because from the surface, a person may see nothing amiss, perhaps âjust a thin wisp of smoke,â Cheyne said, while a meter below the peat burns and can set nearby tree roots aflame, easily toppling them. And peat fires also produce dense, toxic smoke.
Cheyne said since 2015, the foundation and local crews have built over 1,000 dams to block drainage canals, planted almost a million trees, drilled hundreds of water boreholes, and increased support for up to eight fire teams.
âThat preparation is why we are holding,â she said. But itâs still a tenuous situation. For the short-term, Cheyne said, the goal is to keep the firefighting teams in the field fed, equipped and safe, which costs about $100 a day per team. It also means investing in equipment, such as thermal drones that can detect underground peat fires and rewetting the peat, so it doesnât reignite. The foundation, she said, is actively seeking donations from international bodies, advocacy groups and concerned individuals.
While hotspots in Kalimantan have declined since the beginning of the month, according to the foundation, rains are not expected until late October or November.
âWe are not out of this yet,â said Cheyne.
Cheyne said Borneo Nature Foundation Internationalâs co-founder Simon Husson recently passed a troop of monkeys on a river trip and they moved through trees beside mile after mile of burned riverbank.
âThat is the picture,â she said. âLife hanging on right at the edge.â

articles.title_orig: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.title_zh: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.content_orig:
High school students face no shortage of challenges, from maintaining top grades to balancing extracurricular activities. But for Wayzata High School sophomore Aakya Manamperi, her pursuits extend far beyond the classroom. In fact, they stretch all the way across the globe.
Manamperi, 15, is a second-degree black belt and one of the nation’s top-ranked karate competitors in her age group.
Later this fall, she will travel to Spain to compete on the global stage at the World Karate Commission (WKC) World Championships.
Inside Dojo Karate in Medina, Manamperi serves as a patient instructor, guiding young students through fundamental martial arts skills. But don’t let her calm demeanor fool you. When she steps onto the tournament floor, she’s a force to be reckoned with.
“It’s kind of a really male-dominated sport,” Manamperi said. “So, being a female, and a female of color, it’s really important for me to go out there and represent.”
Aakya Manamperi teaches karate to a group of kids at Dojo Karate in Medina.
Manamperi began practicing karate at age 6. Achieving elite national status has required years of rigorous discipline and daily training.
“I’ve been training two hours every single day,” Manamperi said. “The first hour is mostly cardio, training drills, working on technique. And the second hour is just focusing on my kata that I’m going to be competing.”
Kata, her primary discipline, consists of detailed, high-intensity sequences of movements. Judges evaluate performance based on technique, power, rhythm, balance and presentation—an evaluation process that has earned Manamperi an impressive collection of trophies and medals over the years.
Her dedication has drawn praise from local mentors, including Dojo Karate Medina owner Javier Franco, who noted the positive influence she has on younger students.
“Of course, this is a big impact on the students,” Franco said. “They always see their instructors as their heroes.”
A collection of some of the awards Aakya Manamperi has received for her karate expertise.
Manamperi’s drive to make an impact extends beyond martial arts competition. Outside the dojo, she founded The Girl Shield Project , a student-led organization dedicated to empowering young women through self-defense training, leadership development and health education.
“We do online events, we do in-person events, and so far we’ve reached around 200 different girls in around 20 different countries, and hopefully growing to some more,” Manamperi said.
In addition to her athletic and community achievements, Manamperi maintains a 3.99 GPA at Wayzata High School, where she participates in Science Olympiad and Student Council.
As she prepares to represent the United States in Spain, the weight of her accomplishments is not lost on her.
“Honestly, I appreciate it so much,” Manamperi said. “It’s amazing for me to be able to share things that I like to do and my passions with the world and kind of compete in it. It’s something that I still pinch myself to this day about.”

Southern California is expected to see the longest heat wave of the season.
The National Weather Service has issued an extreme heat warning for the greater Los Angeles area from Friday through at least next Thursday, and forecasters say it’ll likely extend beyond that.
Temperatures are expected to be in the mid-90s to mid-100s, even in coastal areas.
“Unfortunately, we don't really see an end to it as far as we can tell, and that's probably the biggest thing we wanna highlight, is that while we have had hotter events this season already, this one might be the longest-lasting,” said Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Kittell said they expect to see a few daily records to be broken.
Southern California saw a record-breaking 10-day heat wave in the summer of 2022 .
Forecasters say conditions likely won’t meet the threshold for issuing red flag warnings (extremely dry air and windy conditions), but the risk of fire is still going to be high during the heat wave.
“It’s still concerning, and if a fire were to get started in the wrong area, it could grow pretty fast,” Kittell said. “ We do have a history of large fires in similar environments with similar heat, similar time of the year.”
As of Thursday afternoon, Southern California Edison said nearly 10,000 customers in parts of Riverside County were under consideration for power shutoffs , which are used to reduce the risk of electrical equipment starting a fire.
In L.A., Orange, San Bernardino, and Riverside counties, call 3-1-1 or call for a list of cooling centers. In the city of Los Angeles, you can also find a list of recreation centers , senior centers and libraries — all good choices for cooling off — online.
You can get more details of cooling centers in Southern California:
Kittell said people should make plans to stay cool during the long heat wave, and check in on neighbors who are elderly, or on families with young children.
Officials say residents should limit outdoor activities to the early morning hours, stay in air-conditioned places in the afternoon and evening hours, and stay hydrated.

articles.title_orig: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.title_zh: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.content_orig:
Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been higher still if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.content_orig:
"You will always be my greatest love story," Blanchard wrote on social media.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard 's partner Kenan Urker was found dead on his 34th birthday in what officials describe as an apparent drug-related incident, authorities said.
Officers discovered Urker dead when they responded to a call from a home in Raceland, Louisiana, on Thursday evening, according to the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office.
Urker, who was lying on a bed, was cold and his face and arms were blue, according to the sheriff's office. A paper towel on his arm appeared to have "blotches of blood" on it, the sheriff's office said.
On the nightstand next to the bed was a holstered handgun, a syringe and two shot glasses, according to the sheriff's office.
In the bathroom, deputies discovered syringes, a spoon and a "brown powdery substance," the sheriff's office said.
The sheriff's office said there's "no evidence of foul play."
Blanchard wrote on Instagram on Friday, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever."
She added in an Instagram story that he was an "amazing father" and "will forever be my soulmate."
In 2015, Blanchard and her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn were arrested for the fatal stabbing of Blanchard's mother, Clauddinnea "Dee Dee" Blanchard.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was released from prison in 2023 .
"Dee Dee" Blanchard had allegedly abused her daughter for years by convincing Gypsy Rose and the public that she was extremely sick, when she wasn't. "Dee Dee" Blanchard allegedly portrayed her daughter as a frail, disabled child who suffered from multiple illnesses including leukemia and muscular dystrophy, subjecting her to a life in a wheelchair, a feeding tube and unnecessary surgeries.
After her release from prison, Gypsy Rose Blanchard told ABC News she wanted to share her story "to bring awareness to mental health issues, to Munchausen by proxy, to abuse victims."
She said she hoped her story would serve as a "cautionary tale" for others.
"So that the next person that might be in a situation like mine, they don't take the route that I did," she said.

articles.title_orig: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.title_zh: How long would it take the world to run out of clothing if production suddenly stopped?
articles.content_orig:
One expert told Marketplace that it could take up to 20 years. People would start tapping into textile waste dumps around the world and, of course, their own closets.
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it ? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here .
Anne Crabbe from Paso Robles, California, asks:
I've always wondered how long it would take for the world to run out of clothes if all production of clothes stopped at once. There are SO many clothes out there (at least here in North America). If the entire world had to use the current supply of all the clothes existing now, when would stores run out? TJ Maxx, Nordstrom Rack, all the thrift stores. I assume (and hope), we would run out of under garments first, then socks, maybe? A ton of assumptions have to be made to answer this, but can it even be answered?
Billions and billions of items of clothing are produced each year, but if clothing production suddenly stopped, snapping up all those garments might take less time than you might think
Depending on your assumptions, it might take up to 20 years for the world to run out of clothing, said Julia DeVoy, who studies the fast-fashion industry and serves as dean of undergraduate programs and students at the Boston College Lynch School of Education and Human Development.
And yes, undergarments and socks would be the first to go, she said.
There would also be a gold rush for materials with higher-quality fiber, like cotton and denim.
"People would want that more, whether it's getting it at a thrift store, or grabbing whatever was on the shelves, or trading with other people who had closets. And there would also be a radical shift towards mending," DeVoy said.
DeVoy estimates that discount and big-box stores in the U.S. would take one month to run out of clothing. These stores operate a just-in time model, which means they only get clothing as needed.
TJX, the parent company of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls, reported its days inventory at 70 days as of mid-2026, which means that shelves would last nine to 10 weeks with zero restocking based on normal demand, DeVoy said. TJX arrives at this figure by taking the existing inventory and dividing it by the current sales rate, DeVoy explained.
But if clothing production stopped, then demand would go up.
"What happened during the pandemic with certain products? People thought they couldn't get hand sanitizer,” DeVoy said. “Basically, what would happen is all the stock on the shelves, because of the just-in-time [model] and the lean inventory that actually sits in the stores, there would be a panic, and all of the existing stock would be wiped out from the store themselves,"
During COVID-19 stockpiling, sales of household staples spiked between 70% to 170% above normal, and spending on stock-up categories ran 70% to 80% above the daily average, DeVoy said.
So if we assume that panic buying doubled demand, which is a conservative estimate, then that would halve the amount of time it would normally take for clothing to run out, leaving discount stores about four to five weeks before clothing ran out, DeVoy said.
People would also look to  thrift stores. Thrift stores are overwhelmed with donations, but they only use about 20% to 30% of the items they receive, DeVoy said. "The remaining 70% to 80% is currently exported, incinerated, or landfilled. This is not because it's all unsellable, but because the humongous volume exceeds available shelf capacity," DeVoy said.
But even if they sold their full backlog instead of incinerating it, DeVoy said they would still sell out in a matter of months.
As stores across the country ran out of clothing, people could tap into other sources that would probably become available. About 100 billion garments are produced a year, with 45 billion garments never reaching the buyer. This is referred to as  "dead stock," which means they're never sold or end up incinerated, DeVoy said.
"There would be this giant hidden reserve that we would keep probably for about the first five years," DeVoy said.
If eight billion people received a modest one to two garments per year, each, that works out to eight to 16 billion garments annually. If there are 45 billion garments, that means there would be three to five years of deadstock, DeVoy said.
There are also massive textile waste dumps around the world, which would now become a vital resource of clothing, and there's a huge surplus of clothing in people's homes, DeVoy said.
The Atacama Desert in Chile receives 131,000 tons of used textiles annually, with over 70%, or 92,000 tons, going directly into landfills or in other illegal dumps, while Ghana's Kantamanto market in Accra receives about 15 million garments a week, of which over 40% becomes direct textile waste, DeVoy said.
"Comparable sites exist all over Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America," DeVoy said.
And people normally only wear 20% of the clothing that they own, with Americans buying 68 new clothing items a year, so they could use the remaining 80% of clothing that's sitting in their closets, DeVoy said.
She estimates that both of these sources of clothing could stretch around 15 years.
One often-cited claim is that we have enough clothing on the planet to last about six generations. But the math and even the original source behind this figure is unclear, according to the BBC, which investigated the claim's origins .
Getting a solid figure is tough – some of those garments in our closet last longer than others, which is just one of the complications that arise when trying to answer this question. "Synthetic fibers tend to last longer and they don't tend to biodegrade very quickly, so we would probably end up with more polyester," said Tasha Lewis, an associate clinical professor in fashion and retail studies at Ohio State University. "We still don't have a good timeline for how long polyester will take to go away because we still have most of it."
We'd also probably think about recycling the clothing that we do have, so we'll still have clothes available to us, Lewis said.
But since clothing production probably won't come to a halt anytime soon, we still have mountains of clothing to deal with. There have been changes in social expectations on how often you should change your clothes and how much variety you should have, said Abigail Clarke-Sather, an associate professor of mechanical and industrial engineering at the University of Minnesota Duluth who's an expert on textile recycling.
"Closet sizes have gotten bigger over the last century because we store so much that we don't know what to do with," Clarke-Sather said.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.title_zh: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight
Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party.
Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!”
In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state . The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol.
“This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing.
Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others.
Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building.
An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens.
Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record.
“This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.”
The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans , all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision.
And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours.
State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments.
“The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson , who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district.
Through continued boos, White said that there was a “ silent majority ” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”.
Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal.
“I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.”
Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”.
“The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.”
Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state.
“If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power.
“We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.”
The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.

articles.title_zh: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
articles.content_orig:
Mac apps will soon need ‘very explicit user action’ to gain full disk access, according to Apple.
Mac apps will soon need ‘very explicit user action’ to gain full disk access, according to Apple.
Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch . In an update on Friday , Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
The change comes just weeks after Inc ’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages , despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone pushed back on this report , saying access to Messages is “entirely opt-in.” Stone added that you have to “enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector for Muse to be able to read your Messages content.”
Now Apple is addressing how developers use that sweeping access, saying:
Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding… As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially.
Full disk access is a permission on macOS that gives an app access to a user’s entire system. Apple says the feature “largely sidesteps” privacy controls offered to users “to allow backup apps to function properly on Mac.” The company doesn’t say when it plans to roll out its update for full disk access. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

articles.title_orig: G7 countries to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves
articles.title_zh: G7 countries to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves
articles.content_orig:
Member countries in the Group of Seven agreed Friday to release tens of millions of barrels of diesel fuel and crude oil, the latest move by industrial economies around the world to cap soaring gas prices.
Following a G7 videoconference hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron, President Donald Trump said, “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil.”
“The process will begin immediately,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
Gas prices have soared since the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. But diesel in particular saw a renewed surge this summer after the Russia-Ukraine war escalated in July. Since late February, the average price of U.S. diesel has surged 70% to $6.37 per gallon.
The release will be as much as 100 million barrels over the course of four months, the G7 said in a statement. It noted that there would be a “substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.”
The leaders also said that they would begin coordinating maintenance schedules for oil refineries in their respective countries, “to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible.”
Many American and European refiners are already operating at maximum capacity levels.
“Our citizens’ concerns about energy prices remain a top priority,” the group said.
Oil analyst Andy Lipow said the release could help smooth over recent supply disruptions.
“A release of 100 million barrels of diesel fuel over four months would essentially replace Russian exports which have been banned as Ukrainian drone strikes have severely reduced Russian refining capacity,” said Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
At the gas pump, he said, “A release of this magnitude could temporarily reduce diesel prices by 25 cents per gallon but does little to increase refinery capacity to produce more.”
In March, countries that are members of the International Energy Agency approved a release of 400 million barrels of crude oil. That helped to partially ease the energy supply crunch for a time, but prices continued to rise.
As of Friday, prices still remain sharply elevated since the Iran war began. Brent crude oil ended the trading day effectively flat at $102.25 per barrel.
Since the start of the year, Brent prices are up more than 60% still.
The agreement between G7 countries also comes after a weeklong pressure campaign by the Trump administration on its European allies, particularly Germany and France, which hold a large share of the European Union’s diesel reserves.
“American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage” alone, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X late Thursday.
With just weeks to go until the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Republicans are facing a wall of poor polling numbers on the economy.
Just 41% of registered voters approve of Trump’s handling of the U.S. economy, according to the most recent NBC News polling, while 56% disapprove.
Meanwhile, economists say Trump’s policies are fueling inflation, roiling financial markets and upending global trade.
Against this backdrop, the president and his party were eager for  a development like Friday’s G7 agreement to help show the public they could make progress on a central election issue: Sky-high gas prices.
But at the same time as Trump is hailing the release of oil and diesel reserves, he has also been openly considering a U.S. diesel export ban.
This would hit E.U. countries, as well as the United Kingdom, particularly hard.
Earlier Friday, the E.U. said it “fully rejects any ban on diesel.”
“A ban would not be beneficial to anyone,” a European Commission spokeswoman told reporters in a briefing.
Following the G7 leaders’ announcement, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said they “welcome the decision of G7 countries not to impose any export bans on allies and the continued solidarity between partners.”
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Florida’s dengue outbreak is now the largest in the continental US in decades
articles.title_zh: Florida’s dengue outbreak is now the largest in the continental US in decades
articles.content_orig:
CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data
Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections.
Hillsborough county, Florida , officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”.
Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said.
Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California.
The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes.
Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases.
Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it.
Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports.
The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. There have been a total of 212 known travel-related cases in Florida reported so far in 2026.
Over the same period, there were 38 locally contracted dengue cases reported in Florida. They were among 190 cases of locally acquired dengue across Florida, the state’s health department said .
Numbers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) differ slightly. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data.
Dengue is contracted through the bite of some mosquito species, largely Aedes aegypti , as well as Aedes albopictus . Both species are present in Florida.
Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain … and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said.
The symptoms typically span four days to one week. A rarer form of the illness called dengue hemorrhagic fever can be fatal without the administration of proper supportive care, the state health department said.
Hillsborough county authorities have expressed optimism that dengue infections might slow down in the coming weeks, with zero “mosquito test pools” testing positive recently, according to the local Bay News 9 outlet.
