articles.title_orig: Trump Directed Use of Taxpayer Money for Ads Praising His Presidency
articles.title_zh: Trump Directed Use of Taxpayer Money for Ads Praising His Presidency
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has created at least 13 campaign-style ads as part of its controversial taxpayer-funded, multi-million-dollar effort to promote President Donald Trump and his policies.
Yet-to-be-aired spots include a trio of ads highlighting the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela, one called “God Made Trump” and another recapping the UFC fight he hosted at the White House. Republicans and Democrats alike have questioned the wisdom of spending so much taxpayer money on the ads, which the White House has defended as public service announcements.
CNN has obtained clips of 12 ads, which range from 15 seconds to three minutes long, including two that have already aired. They appear in a Dropbox account — which was shared with CNN — run by LMD, the agency that has been given the government contract for the ad buys. Each ends with “Paid for by the U.S. Government” at the bottom of the screen. Another ad that is not in the Dropbox account, “Final Battle,” has also aired in recent weeks.
The three ads that have already aired have appeared on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. It’s not clear if all of the ads will air on television or digital platforms.
Asked for comment, the White House on Friday afternoon pointed to a just-posted video compilation of the president criticizing CNN.
While each of the ads has a different theme, many of them include imagery of the president and audio with positive reviews from news reports, which is likely to intensify criticism that the campaign is using taxpayer dollars to help Trump personally. They also include patriotic images — including the cap toss at a military graduation, fireworks over Mount Rushmore and military flyovers.
First lady Melania Trump, who has been a rare presence at the White House during the president’s second term, is featured in many of the ads. There are also images from Trump’s reciprocal tariff announcement, the border wall, his escalator presidential-campaign announcement and the tongue-in-cheek framed photograph of an auto pen signifying former President Joe Biden on Trump’s “Presidential Walk of Fame.”
CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said that they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.
The ads that have aired so far have spurred widespread condemnation, even as the White House indicates it plans to ramp up its efforts. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.” If Democrats win control of the House next year, he’ll gain congressional subpoena power.
Even some Republicans have criticized the ad campaign.
“Look, if you want to spend money out of your super PAC or other campaign account to communicate that message, that’s fine. It’s not an appropriate PSA. It’s just not, you know, it’s not how we should be spending taxpayer dollars,” said Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina.
Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has said “no” the ads are not an appropriate use of taxpayer dollars. “It’s not even a close question.”
The “UFC 250” ad heavily promotes the company and the June fight that Trump hosted at the White House, prominently featuring UFC CEO Dana White as well as the fighters, the lit-up “claw” over the Octagon and the championship belt.
The “Maduro” spot intersperses a speech by Nicolas Maduro with appearances by Trump and his team at Mar-a-Lago following the Venezuelan dictator’s capture.
And “Military Hype” shows images of fighter jets and unclassified video of what appears to be missile launches. It also includes Trump’s February speech announcing the war with Iran, a conflict which remains deeply unpopular with the American people.
“This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump says in the ad, now seven months into the war.
Some of the ads are starkly political: The two-minute “King of the Jungle” video features images of Trump’s perceived political enemies — former Presidents Barack Obama and Biden, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, all Democrats. There’s video of lions hunting in the wild and a bald eagle sweeping down on the water. A cover of “In the Air Tonight” by In This Moment plays. And Christopher Walken’s lion speech from the 2002 film, “Poolhall Junkies,” is interspersed.
One of the spots, a three-minute-long ad titled “God Made Trump,” was broadcast during Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas. In it, Trump is presented as a messianic figure with a riff on Paul Harvey’s “God Made a Farmer.” It was created by Dilley Meme Team, according to NPR , and began going viral earlier this year.
“I need somebody with arms strong enough to rustle the deep state, and yet gentle enough to deliver his own grandchild. Somebody to ruffle the feathers,” the voiceover says, “So God made Trump.”
The ad “Resilience” shows Trump at multiple points in his life, including early in his New York real estate career, an appearance he made on “The Oprah Winfrey Show,” his descent down the Trump Tower escalator as he announced his candidacy in 2015 and then his time at the White House. In the audio, a reporter refers to him as “the bodyguard of Western Civilization.” His 2023 mugshot from a Fulton County, Georgia, sheriff’s office features prominently, along with video of an assassination attempt on him in Butler, Pennsylvania.
At least an estimated $5.6 million in taxpayer dollars have already been spent on the ads, according to a leading political ad-tracking firm, AdImpact. The actual cost of the taxpayer-funded ad campaign is even higher, but can’t be fully ascertained because public service announcements are subject to different public disclosure rules than campaign ads.
A total of $20 million has been allocated for the effort. The money for these ads is coming from Customs and Border Protection, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Watchdog groups have said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications, but it’s not clear if outside groups have standing to file a lawsuit. Though the ads have received bipartisan criticism, Congress — which groups said had the clearest lane to provide some accountability — has not acted to block the ads.

The facts about what happened aboard Flydubai flight 1073 , from Dubai, UAE  to Tel Aviv, Israel on Sept. 30 are not in dispute. The plane, carrying more than 170 passengers, left the ground at 3:05 a.m. local time (11:05 p.m. EDT) to begin a planned three-hour and 35-minute journey, climbing to a cruising altitude of 34,000 ft., according to FlightRadar24 , a live air traffic site. At 5:21 a.m., the co-pilot, an unnamed Omani national, attacked the pilot, an Indian national named Smit Machchhar, with what is being variously described as an axe or a knife.
The plane went into a steep dive, plummeting more than 14,000 ft. in 30 seconds, slinging screaming passengers from their seats. Bleeding profusely from cuts to his hands and head, Machchhar managed to send out three alerts to the ground: a so-called 7700 alarm, indicating a “general emergency;” then a 7500, indicating “unlawful interference;” then another 7700. More importantly, he was able to unlatch and open the locked cockpit door, tumbling into the galley area at the front of the plane, while still wrestling with his co-pilot.
Two passengers and one flight crew member subdued the attacker and bound his hands with the cables from passenger headphones. In a case of good fortune, two reserve pilots were aboard the plane, there to relieve the prime crew when they landed in Tel Aviv. The pair raced to the cockpit, took the controls, and landed the plane safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. Both of the prime pilots were taken to a local hospital, where Machchhar is being treated for his wounds, and the attacker was taken into custody, where he faced interrogation by Saudi law enforcement officers before being handed over to the UAE.
In an interview with Fox News , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it was too soon to know if the co-pilot were acting in coordination with Iran, with which Israel is currently at war, in an act of organized terrorism, “but he obviously hated Israelis because he was going to kill about 170 of them on the plane, killing himself too.”
U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday suggested the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what [he's] hearing," but did not provide any details.
Machchhar, meantime, is being hailed a hero on the international stage. “Captain Smit Machchhar has shown the world the highest form of courage,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted on X . “Without fearing for his own life, he fought valiantly and prevented another 9/11 like attack from happening.”
What’s far less clear in the wake of the near mass casualty is how it happened in the first place. The attacker had been with the airline for eight months —coming aboard before the war in Iran began. Was he nonetheless collaborating with Iran, or was he a self-radicalized lone wolf? What kind of screening do commercial pilots worldwide go through to ensure mental stability and to rule out terrorist or criminal links? How did a weapon make it aboard the plane in the first place? And are the locked and hardened cockpit doors—which went into use on airlines worldwide after 9/11—almost too secure, keeping attackers out, yes, but preventing rescuers from getting in to stop a similar incident between pilots?
The early reports that the weapon used in the attack was a knife raised questions, since the popular belief is that pilots and crew go through the same security screening passengers do. But that’s not the case, according to experts.
“Most of the pilots and flight crew will go through what's called the ‘crew member access point,’” says Jeff Price, professor of aviation at the Metropolitan State University of Denver, and author of the book Practical Aviation Security . “They’re called ‘known crew members.’ A large part of this is based on trust. They have access to the airplane and if they wanted to sabotage it, they probably could.”
Subsequent investigations revealed that the co-pilot did not have a knife, but instead used what’s known as a crash axe , a tool kept in the cockpit for use, as its name suggests, as a means of escape or rescue in the event of an accident.
Other kinds of screening—for mental health, criminal background, and potential association with terrorist or other criminal organizations—is more rigorous, but standards vary from country to country. “A new pilot does go through a criminal history record check to see if they've ever been arrested or convicted of a set of 28 different crimes,” says Price of the U.S. process. “They also go through what's called a security threat assessment, which is a TSA check to see if they are on any sort of list that might require them to not receive a badge to the airline, which means they can't fly for the airline.”
Psychological profiling is much less strict, basically operating on the honor system—honor being a quality that somebody with an eye toward bringing down a plane would not be likely to possess in abundance. “There's not a federal requirement for that other than their flight medical [tests], in which case they're given a questionnaire that basically says, ‘Are you mentally stable and do feel okay?’” says Price.
International standards do call for, at a minimum, this level of mental health screening, but standards and enforcement vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.
Flydubai passengers arriving in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Sept. 30, 2026. Nir Keidar/Anadolu—Getty Images
As for locked cockpit doors, they can be opened from the outside provided that somebody knows the combination—which, outside of the pilots themselves, only firefighters, police, and other first responders do. That, Price admits, does raise the question of the doctrine of unintended consequences, with the post-9/11 security measures solving one problem while creating another.
Additionally, in the U.S., new Federal Aviation Administration rules require what is called a “secondary cockpit barrier” on all newly-manufactured commercial planes delivered to U.S. airlines. The rule, which doesn’t apply to existing planes, is set to add an extra layer of security at the head of the plane and, hopefully, prevent any potential bad actors from gaining access to the cockpit. But again, what if the danger lies within the cockpit?
“Everything we did was to try and prevent access to the flight deck, which doesn't do a whole lot of good when the problem is coming from inside the house,” acknowledges Price, adding that “it’s a [matter of] risk-reward.”
On balance, the risk of another such mutinous crew member trying to commandeer a plane is less than the reward that comes from preventing hijackers from seizing the cockpits as they did aboard four flights 25 years ago. But the danger of an incident like yesterday’s ending catastrophically is decidedly nonzero.
Price cites the tragic case of Germanwings Flight 9525 which crashed on March 24, 2015, taking the lives of 150 people, when the pilot left the cockpit to use the restroom and the co-pilot took that opportunity to seize the plane and fly it into the French Alps.
“It has almost never happened,” Price says, “but it has happened.”

articles.title_orig: California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules
articles.title_zh: California Sues to Block Trump From Weakening Fuel Economy Rules
articles.content_orig:
Twenty-six states, including California and New York, have filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump’s administration after the US Department of Transportation lowered fuel economy standards for petrol-powered vehicles.
The lawsuit, filed on Friday, challenges the Department of Transportation’s rollback of fuel economy standards to a fleet average fuel economy of 34.9 miles (56km) per gallon (3.78 litres) by model year 2031. Under the administration of former President Joe Biden, fuel economy standards were set at 50.4 miles (81km) per gallon by model year 2031.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is leading the lawsuit, argued that the Trump administration improperly changed how federal regulators calculate fuel economy standards.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) bases standards on technological improvements that could make petrol-powered vehicles more efficient. To do that, it first models the current fleet’s performance and then considers what additional actions manufacturers could take to improve their fuel economy in future model years above that.
In past standards, including during the first Trump administration, NHTSA’s baseline fleet included the millions of electric vehicles that already run on US roads.
Bonta said the Transportation Department change ignores the existing slate of EVs, which makes it easier to justify weaker standards for petrol-powered vehicles, and called the approach “flawed” and “dramatically distorted”.
The lawsuit also alleges that NHTSA’s new rule is contrary to law and that NHTSA contravenes its mandate from Congress to set fuel-economy standards at their “maximum feasible” level.
The Transportation Department has said the change could save American taxpayers $138bn over the next five years.
“The president started a war that has created volatility in oil markets, disrupted global energy supplies, and left families and businesses paying the price at the pump. Yet, the Trump administration is attempting to gut fuel economy standards and force Americans to spend billions more on gas while poisoning the air in our communities,” Attorney General Bonta said in a statement.
The rollback was applauded by car makers.
“We welcome the Administration’s efforts to reset the CAFE [Corporate Average Fuel Economy] regulations to more achievable targets that are better aligned with market realities,” said Shane Karr, senior vice president of public affairs at Stellantis North America.
The litigation by the states came in tandem with a second lawsuit filed on Friday by progressive and climate groups, including the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen.
“Trump’s lawless push to roll back key safeguards on fuel economy will pollute our air, and line the pockets of oil and auto CEOs. We are confident of stopping Trump’s CAFE standards rollback,” Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen said in a statement announcing the lawsuit, which was filed in a federal court in Washington DC.
Auto stocks were trending downward throughout the day, with Ford, General Motors and Toyota closing down around 1 percent. Stellantis fell more than 6 percent amid reports of slumping sales.

articles.title_orig: Musk-led war commission triggers alarms in Pentagon
articles.title_zh: Musk-led war commission triggers alarms in Pentagon
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Army is standing up a new command and a new acquisition office dedicated to further prioritizing autonomous technolog y, according to a service spokesperson and a memo reviewed by Breaking Defense.
The changes, first reported by Axios , come on the heels of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s newly announced initiatives at the Pentagon to create a new four-star command, called Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM), centered on drones and similar technology as well as a new working group on the future of defense.
According to a Thursday memo reviewed by Breaking Defense and signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle , orders the creation of the Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.
“Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made it clear: We are done with the bureaucratic inertia holding back modernization,” T elle said in a statement provided to Breaking Defense tod ay. “The Army is rapidly advancing to maintain our lethal edge. We are forging the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command to get cutting-edge technology into the hands of Soldiers, while prioritizing autonomy in our formations, our acquisitions, and our training to dominate the future of warfare.”
The memo also designates a new Program Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Autonomy. Currently , the service’s autonomy efforts are under Capability Portfolio Executive Mission Autonomy, which falls under PAE Layered Protection and Integration. Also outlined in the memo, titled, “Army Autonomous Initiatives,”  is the decision to conduct new “autonomous force development[s]” to create force structure that can align with autonomous capabilities in aviation, armored and sustainment and training formations.  The memo also orders the new PAE to “prioritize the acquisition and fielding of” autonomous fires, combat vehicles, watercraft resupply, manned and unmanned platform collaborative teaming and more “no later than” fiscal 2028.
Lastly, the order states that the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower and Reserve Affairs will expand the authorizations of the service’s 15X, which is th e new tactical unmanned aircraft systems specialist unit, and the 390A unit, which is the robotics technician specialist unit, “to all applicable Army units.”
The Army’s push to establish a new command and PAE, coupled with Hegseth’s plans to establish AUTOWARCOM, come as part of a larger effort to scale drone production and push those weapons out to the force. That push has included the Drone Dominance program to buy more aerial weapons, the creation of the Army-led Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) and, as first reported by Breaking Defense, the creation of Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DRPM) for autonomy.

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg AI Garage prepares business students to solve real-world problems with agentic AI
articles.content_orig:
The rapidly expanding capabilities and applications of AI has created a new frontier in higher education. As it is more widely integrated into industry and becoming a highly desired skill, universities are faced with finding effective and ethical ways of teaching the technology and preparing their students for a more technologically savvy workplace.
“Our students are going out into the workplace, and they’re entering a bit of a storm,” said Price Jett, University of Lynchburg’s chief financial officer.
“AI is the highest impacting tool set that we can use to give lifts to businesses. … But it dawned on me that our students are ill prepared, and maybe even some of our professors [are] unaware of what’s going on. … So, we came up with this concept called the [AI] Garage.”
The AI Garage is an agentic AI laboratory where selected students can experiment with building AI agents to solve a company’s real business problems. Jett and Dr. Timothy Schauer, dean of the School of Professional and Applied Sciences, launched the AI Garage as an experiment in the Spring of 2026.
The project brought together businesses, students, and industry experts who Schauer and Jett referred to as “thought accelerators.”
“We talk about ethics — we talk about responsibility — but this isn’t just basic AI where you’re using it to write your papers for you,” said Schauer. “We want it to accomplish things that can be done behind the scenes so that the human doesn’t have to do it, but still stays in the loop.”
Agentic AI goes beyond the generative large language models, such as ChatGPT or Gemini, which typically create content in response to a prompt. Given a goal, an AI agent can determine the necessary steps, use connected tools, and perform tasks independently within defined rules, without requiring a new prompt at every stage. Depending on its purpose and permissions, an agent could analyze data, research information, send emails, schedule meetings, update records, or monitor a process and adjust its actions until the goal is met, all with a “persistent” memory capability similar to a human co-worker.
Of the nearly 30 students who showed interest in joining the pilot cohort, only seven were selected. Working in teams, the students spent four weeks at the end of the spring semester creating solutions to the real-world problems provided to them by four business executives.
The AI Garage was set up in Schewel Hall on special computers that were not connected to the University’s network. Schauer and Jett worked closely with Lynchburg’s IT department when setting up the lab to create a “walled garden” where the students would be able to safely work with their AI agents.
The students selected for the Garage had to be dedicated to the work, willing to put in the necessary time and effort even while finishing their course work and preparing for final exams and projects.
“These students were in this room — they ate there, some of them slept there,” said Schauer. “We’d come in in the morning, sometimes they worked all night. They were there on the weekends. They were very motivated.”
One of these students was Kristofer Hickson ʼ26, a veteran who transferred to Lynchburg after completing his associate degree at Central Virginia Community College.
“I’m not a computer science person,” said Hickson, a business major. “I have trouble finding my way around my own email. … [but] I can stumble my way around things and find my way into it.”
Hickson began experimenting with generative AI as he searched for work, using large language models, or LLMs, to refine and improve his resumes and cover letters so they better aligned with a given job description. Over time he became exhausted with manually prompting the LLM to do this work so he asked it to create a program that would do it automatically and upload and export to a file on his computer.
A few months before the AI Garage was launched, Hickson explained what he had been doing to Dr. Eric Kyper, a professor of business and economics. Kyper recognized that Hickson had stumbled into agentic AI and through their conversation, Hickson began thinking about what pursuing agentic AI could mean for his future.
Khurshid Kazimi ʼ28, an accounting major, was another student in the first AI Garage cohort. When she learned about the project, she immediately jumped at the opportunity.
“The first two weeks of working on building the AI agent was so difficult,” said Kazimi, an international student from Afghanistan. “And one thing that I realized later was that Price Jett and Dr. Schauer — they were not sharing all the information with us. … We were completely lost.”
Kazimi explained that Schauer and Jett wanted the students to take initiative and have the curiosity to figure out the next steps on their own. She was appreciative of the approach they took, saying, “They did the absolute best thing.”
She was also appreciative of her fellow students and the various talents each brought to the AI Garage.
“When we’re working together, we can find out the things that we cannot find out when we’re working alone,” Kazimi said.
“We were working on the same thing [and] I was not realizing a problem,” she explained. “I didn’t have that mindset to look at the problem in the same way … and then my teammate — she was finding out the thing that I couldn’t.”
At the end of the four-week period, the students presented their work to executives from each company. All of the companies involved wanted to use the tools the students created for them.
“The goal was not to give something valuable to a company, although that happened,” said Jett. “The goal [was] to teach our students how to solve business problems and give lift to businesses. That’s what businesses expect from us at the University.
“I think that’s our responsibility as leaders at the University to do that.”
Schauer added, “I do think that those universities that teach [AI] responsibly will put their students in a better position to actually get jobs and create value for companies. You can’t ignore that.”
Three students, including Hickson and Kazimi, were immediately offered internships or full-time employment.
“[Companies] don’t want people with computer science degrees,” said Hickson. “They want people with accounting skills, business skills, marketing skills, who know how to use agentic AI.”
He added, “I got a lot of confidence because [of] everything I built from scratch in the [AI] Garage. … It got me where I’m at and has helped give me the confidence to tread a little further.”
Schauer and Jett are now running the second round of the AI Garage this semester with four new businesses. For more information about the AI Garage, contact Schauer at [email protected] .

articles.title_orig: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.title_zh: Littleton students become junior journalists for World News Day
articles.content_orig:
The Goddard School of Littleton celebrated World News Day by transforming students into “junior journalists” for a day on Sept. 28
For one day, students at The Goddard School of Littleton became junior journalists.
Wearing ties and carrying cardboard microphones, children interviewed classmates as part of the school’s first World News Day celebration. The activity was designed to encourage curiosity and help students practice asking questions.
“World News Day really ties into our curriculum that focuses on teaching the students how we ask questions,” said Erin Davis, co-owner of The Goddard School of Littleton. “It asks how we can dive a bit deeper and be investigative.”
The Goddard School of Littleton is a private early childhood education program serving infants, toddlers, preschoolers and pre-kindergarten students. Nearly 700 Goddard Schools locations across the country participated in World News Day this year, according to Chas Kurtz, the organization’s senior public relations manager.
“The idea came from a natural connection we saw between young children and journalists: both are constantly asking questions to better understand the world around them,” Kurtz said.
Becoming a “junior journalist” embodies The Goddard School’s Wonder of Learning program, which is an inquiry-based program that employs a STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math) approach to its curriculum.
“(World News Day) also gave us an opportunity to bring Wonder of Learning to life because inquiry-based learning isn’t simply about arriving at the ‘right’ answer; it's about helping children learn how to think, explore and continue asking questions,” Kurtz said.
In The Goddard School of Littleton’s gym, kids lined up outside the hallway and were granted permission to enter by their teacher one by one. They sat and waited for instruction from their team of teachers — usually a pair or group comprised of a lead and assistant teacher.
On the walls were different stations for the students to explore. One station was a press conference set up with a table and props.
Students took turns sitting at the table and answering questions from their peers, like “How is your day?” and “What are you going to be for Halloween?”
Davis, who runs and owns the Littleton school with her husband, Andrew, said each class had its own lesson plan revolved around journalism.
“Our toddlers had newspaper prints to get that exposure to real-world materials,” Davis said.
Jess Reynolds, one of the directors at the Goddard School of Littleton, helped arrange the gym for World News Day to go beyond lesson planning, Davis said.
“It works because it’s a combination of taking what maybe couldn’t fully come to fruition in a classroom and building a better space for that,” she said of the gym activities.
Two children and Jess Reynolds, a director at the Goddard School of Littleton, sit at the press conference table in the gym on Sept. 28
As the kids rotated between being the interviewer and the interviewee, Reynolds and Davis hopped around different classrooms to help and see what the students were up to. Reynolds, who also works on social media promotion for the school, took videos of two students talking about their weekends and asking each other questions.
“It’s awesome to see what they come up with and see them think through their questions and answers,” she said.
In the class with 2-year-olds, they colored in comics and food illustrations for a food review column.
Other classes had a map of the state with clouds, a sun, and raindrops to experience meteorology reporting.
Asking questions gives children power, Kurtz said.
“Asking ‘why,’ ‘how’ or ‘what if’ is one of the ways children learn to make sense of the world. And when they ask a question, listen to someone else’s perspective, investigate an idea and share what they discover, they’re building skills that extend far beyond journalism,” he said. “They’re learning to think critically, communicate, problem-solve and remain curious.”
According to Davis, helping students grasp the basics of various media forms, ranging from news articles to television programming, is important.
That fundamental principle inspired the creation of World News Day: the belief that journalists bear the responsibility of delivering trustworthy news and information essential to supporting both citizens and a democratic society.
World News Day is celebrated annually on Sept. 28, and The Goddard School may continue its junior journalist trend next year.
“We’ve especially loved seeing the celebration extend beyond the classroom by connecting local media with our students and staff and bringing our wider communities together to celebrate journalism,” Kurtz said. “We’re looking forward to learning from this year’s experience and exploring how we can build on our World News Day celebration in the future.”
Davis said after World News Day wraps up for The Goddard School of Littleton, she would be interested in celebrating again next year.
“One of the great things about our curriculum and our teachers is that we can try new things and grow them every time and focus on adaptability,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.title_zh: Real-World Evidence and Long-Term Data for Lybalvi and Aristada
articles.content_orig:
Real-world data show Lybalvi cuts acute care visits in schizophrenia or bipolar I with AUD, while long-acting aripiprazole offers flexible dosing and stable symptom control.
Retrospective claims analysis data showed significant reductions in hospital and emergency department visits after initiation of Lybalvi (olanzapine/samidorphan) among patients with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder and comorbid alcohol use disorder (AUD), according to Hemangi Panchmatia, MS. Acute care events were measured in 4 categories: all-cause, mental health–related, disease-related, and AUD-related. "We saw a significant reduction across all of these 4 categories in our schizophrenia patients as well as bipolar I disorder patients who have a comorbid alcohol use disorder," Panchmatia said.
Samidorphan, an opioid antagonist with strong binding at the mu receptor, was combined with olanzapine to attenuate weight gain and metabolic dysfunction. Peripheral effects included glucose metabolism and fat accumulation, whereas central effects on the brain's reward system may have supported satiety and reduced cravings.  Antecedent studies fed into a long-term open-label extension lasting up to 4 years or beyond for many patients, and mitigation of weight gain and metabolic dysfunction was associated with better adherence and longer persistence. 1 Many patients had no significant weight gain, and metabolic parameters remained stable over a long period. Findings extended across schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder and across patients early in illness and those more typical of clinical trials. "It's important to provide your patients with an efficacious treatment that they can adhere to, that they can tolerate, and that they will stay on for long periods of time," McGrory said.
A separate clinician-focused poster summarized the development program for aripiprazole lauroxil, a long-acting injectable prodrug formulated to reduce absorption. This design allowed extended release with consistent, predictable plasma concentrations and without pronounced peak and trough effects, maintaining patients at levels relevant to their symptoms. Dosing once monthly, every 6 weeks, or every 2 months allowed clinicians to individualize intervals. Significant symptom reductions were observed on the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale, with improvement on the Clinical Global Impression–Severity scale. 2 The adverse event profile mirrored that of oral aripiprazole over an extended period, including low sedation and lower levels of metabolic dysfunction and weight gain.

articles.title_orig: France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
articles.title_zh: France: 400 schools closed as student protests continue
articles.content_orig:
Over 400 schools and colleges across France remained closed on Friday as student protests over education-related grievances continued — with some turning violent.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told reporters that 735 teaching establishments were "affected" in some way on Friday, "30% fewer than yesterday."
He said that three emergency services personnel had been injured responding, again an improvement on "31 yesterday," and condemned occasional "acts of extreme violence" among the wider protest movement.
The protests ​against teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and a lack of learning materials erupted at lycées (equivalent to US high schools) in the Paris region last month before spreading across the country this week.
Government ministers tried to strike a balance between empathetic messages to frustrated youth with presidential elections looming, and clear calls for calm in their public messaging.
"Calm must urgently return to high schools and universities," Europe and Foreign Affairs Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said online. "Yes, the right to demonstrate is inalienable. But the violence is inexcusable, and the cynical instrumentalization of youth for political ends is irresponsible."
Some of the roughly 400 schools or colleges that closed had sustained damage amid the demonstrations, with one of the worst hit being the Lycee Mandela in Nantes, which was expected to be out of action until mid-October after a fire in the entrance hall.
Police have made around 2,000 arrests and scores of people have been injured, including 40 high school principals, according to Geffray.
Fires were started in at least two high schools on Thursday, while teachers were reportedly inadvertently ​splashed with petrol ⁠at a third in the southern city of Marseille, according to officials.
At ​least one car was torched in the eastern city of Strasbourg while riot police clashed with youths in Toulouse in the southwest.
In the southeastern region of Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, authorities claimed that "at least €25 million" of damage has been done in their jurisdiction alone. The Ile de France region that includes Paris estimated damages around €7 million on Friday.
But students have also criticized what they see as a heavy-handed police response.
"You don't want to hear our words; you just fire tear gas," one student wrote on a placard outside the Lycée Voltaire in central Paris.
Minister Geffray told broadcasters on Friday morning that "violent individuals" were "infiltrating groups of students" and "taking the movement hostage" and called on parents to prevent their children from joining the protests.
"What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger," he said.
Geffray met with student representatives and trade unions later on Friday. After this meeting, student group leaders renewed their call for "concrete" responses to their demands, said the protests should continue, but also appealed to demonstrators to refrain from any violence or vandalism.
"If I could address a clear message to high schoolers: be smart. We are giving, once again, cause to those who wish to instrumentalize and discredit our cause. Be non-violent," Nahanael Combary of the Renouveau Lycéen group said.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
According to Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, French domestic intelligence agencies told a crisis meeting on Thursday that the movement has been instrumentalized by politicians from the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) – who have denied the allegations.
Veteran LFI leader and 2027 presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has indeed supported the protests but called on students to use non-violent methods.
"Students, teachers and educational staff are facing the same state of neglect and their positions and claims should be respected," he wrote in a statement earlier this week, calling for "disciplined struggle, no panic, no irritation."
Meanwhile, student union bodies have called for a day of mass protest next Tuesday, October 6, under the slogan: "Police out of schools! No to the repression of student mobilization!"
"The police have no place in front of educational establishments," read a statement. "We support the ongoing mobilization and call for it to be reinforced."

NEW YORK (WABC) -- The Cornell rape accuser was "failed" by people obligated to protect her, including police and the prosecutor, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said at a news conference on Friday.
A visibly outraged Hochul blasted Cornell University Police, the Tompkins County district attorney and the state's rape laws before introducing Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the controversial case
James told a packed news conference at the governor's office that this is now "an active criminal investigation." She pledged a full and fair investigation.
"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard, that is the promise of our justice system," James said.
Hochul said the system failed Jane Doe. Information from her interview with police was not passed to the district attorney, who then failed to interview her.
"I am deeply disturbed by Cornell University's police and how they handled this," Hochul said. She said sending a "partial record" to the district attorney was a failure.
"In what world would the police learn from the victim that she had literally been gang raped" and that she believed "100%" she had been raped and not elevate those allegations, Hochul said.
Hochul claimed the Tompkins County district attorney then did not do the "bare minimum" and interview the woman after receiving the six-page police report.
"In what world does the district attorney not interview her or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked again. That is "exactly why we're here today and why I took the action last night ."
Tompkins County District Attorney Matt Van Houten told ABC News that CUPD's six-page summary of Jane Doe's allegations convinced him no crime occurred.
Hochul also took the opportunity to call for a change in the state law around voluntary intoxication in cases of sexual assault. She said lawmakers must address this part of the law as soon as possible.
Jane Doe's attorney said he and his client are "pleased" the governor appointed a special prosecutor because "contradictions between the district attorney's statements and those of the Cornell police have been shocking."
Van Houten said Friday he supports the governor's decision to remove him from the case and pledged his cooperation with the attorney general.
Cornell has also endorsed Hochul's decision to remove the DA from the case and assign it to James.
"We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State's rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case," a spokesperson said.

Falcon Heavy launched its first NRO mission while SpaceX landed four boosters in one day.
SpaceX closed out one of its busiest days ever with a midnight Falcon Heavy launch from Florida, and the rocket’s two side boosters came home to finish off a landing record the company had never set before.
Falcon Heavy lifted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:54 p.m. ET Thursday carrying NROL-97, a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office. It was the first time the NRO has flown on Falcon Heavy after 22 missions on Falcon 9, and the first NRO mission bought through the National Security Space Launch Phase 3 Lane 2 contract awarded in 2025, according to Spaceflight Now .
Falcon Heavy lifts off from pad 39A in Florida for the 14th time! pic.twitter.com/uuZLKNTdD7
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
Roughly eight minutes after liftoff, side boosters B1104 and B1072 touched down at Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, setting off double sonic booms across Brevard County. B1104 was flying for the second time and B1072 for the fourth. Both last flew on August 30 on NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, making NROL-97 the quickest turnaround between Falcon Heavy missions to date. The brand new center core, B1106, was expended in the Atlantic so the payload could reach its high energy orbit, and SpaceX’s mission page noted the fairing had previously flown on the NROL-95 mission in July.
The two landings capped a record for SpaceX. Earlier Thursday, Falcon 9 booster B1101 returned to Landing Zone 40 after sending the Crew-13 astronauts to the International Space Station , and another Falcon 9 launched the Transporter-18 rideshare with 130 payloads from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Spaceflight Now reported it was the first time SpaceX has landed four boosters in a single day, wrapping up the triple header Teslarati previewed on Wednesday .
Falcon Heavy’s side boosters land on LZ-1 and LZ-2 pic.twitter.com/dBPcNeggFx
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) October 2, 2026
The mission also brought Landing Zone 1 back for what may be its final landing. SpaceX first landed an orbital class booster there in December 2015, but its lease on the former Launch Complex 13 site ended in 2025 as the company moved Florida landings to new pads at its own launch complexes. With LZ-40 already holding the Crew-13 booster, SpaceX brought LZ-1 back into service for one more night. Launch tracker Next Spaceflight listed NROL-97 as the final expected landing at the site.
NROL-97 adds to a fast growing stack of national security work for SpaceX. The company has flown four Space Force missions from Vandenberg since mid August, several believed to carry Starshield satellites, pushing its Pentagon contract total for 2026 past $8 billion . Elon Musk was also named this week to help lead the Pentagon’s Project Meridian study on the future of warfare.
The Florida doubleheader stood out for another reason. The Space Coast saw only one launch in all of September as SpaceX shifts more of its East Coast infrastructure toward Starship, which reached orbit for the first time on Flight 14 just three days earlier.

Tesla Full Self-Driving is set to receive improvements to address its two biggest issues, according to a company engineer.
Director of Engineering at Tesla AI, Phil Duan, revealed in a post on X that improvements to both pothole avoidance and navigation “are coming,’ something we have heard many times in the past. However, there are a few things that seem to hint that things might be different this time around.
Improvements on both are coming.

Pothole avoidance, navigation, speed control, and left lane camping are some of the most prevalent and frequently mentioned shortcomings of the Full Self-Driving suite. These are a few of the biggest issues that have kept Tesla Full Self-Driving as a Supervised suite, meaning drivers must remain attentive during operation .
Pothole avoidance was first mentioned as an “Upcoming Improvement” with the Tesla Full Self-Driving v14.3 update back in early April of this year. It was listed alongside “Expand reasoning to all behaviors beyond destination handling.”
Tesla is fixing Full Self-Driving’s pothole problem
It’s been six months since we first saw pothole avoidance explicitly mentioned , and it has not moved beyond that and joined the main release notes yet.
Tesla has not shed any light on why pothole avoidance has been such an issue for it to solve, but it also has issues identifying large bumps much of the time, so its modeling of sudden changes in road conditions is likely pretty weak at this particular point. I’ve had more issues with large bumps than potholes, personally, but both are issues that need to be resolved.
This is that big bounce that I mentioned in the quoted post.

It makes sense that things might be pretty close to being released to the public, as we are going on such an extensive period of time between it being mentioned and it actually being deployed.
Navigation is likely the most painful part of using Full Self-Driving , as it routinely takes strange routes, has trouble with local rules (like Except Right Turn Stop Signs in Pennsylvania), and sometimes does not realize that maneuvers it is suggesting are against the law. Turning out of my neighborhood, you cannot turn left, yet my Model Y still suggests it roughly 70 percent of the time when I’m leaving.
However, Tesla might be close to a breakthrough on this . With the Summer Update, Tesla added “Preferred Routes” alongside “Automatic Navigation.”
Preferred Routes prioritized roads that the driver had actually taken before, instead of always defaulting to what the vehicle believes is the most efficient path. This has already solved many of my issues. Formerly, I would turn off the Online Routing setting, and that would eliminate most of my complaints with routing, but then you lose out later on the Live Traffic Visualization.
Tesla’s Navigation has improved tremendously thanks to the Preferred Routes release with the Summer Update, but it still could use some polishing , as it still suggests strange routes from time to time, and it also has a lot of issues getting out of a parking lot. articles.title_orig: When should I get the flu shot? What experts say is the ideal time to protect yourself
articles.title_zh: When should I get the flu shot? What experts say is the ideal time to protect yourself
articles.content_orig:
Should you get your flu shot with a Covid vaccine? Here’s the guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
It’s October and time for flu shots.
Medical experts urge getting a flu vaccination soon, before influenza starts spreading widely — and to get up to date on protection against other fall respiratory viruses, too. Updated COVID-19 shots are available now, plus shots for people especially vulnerable to another winter risk called RSV.
Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
While these infections make many people feel miserable for a few days before they recover, every year flu alone causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations in the U.S. and kills tens of thousands.
Vaccination isn’t “a guarantee that we’re going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk” of the worst outcomes, said Dr. Ryan Stanton of the American College of Emergency Physicians.
Fall vaccine advice usually comes from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and its independent advisory panel. But this year that panel, which influences state and insurance vaccine policies, is caught in a court battle and the CDC hasn't updated its advice.
Now doctors’ groups are filling the gap: the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America have posted vaccination guidelines for their patient populations plus the scientific evidence behind them.
Just about everybody starting at age 6 months needs flu vaccination, the medical societies agree. But flu is particularly dangerous for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems, including asthma, diabetes, heart disease and weak immune systems. The last two flu seasons brought unusually high numbers of child deaths, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated kids.
The vaccines don't block all flu infections, but they do help prevent the worst outcomes, decreasing older adults' hospitalizations by 31% last year, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project, a public health group based at the University of Minnesota.
Three “enhanced” flu vaccines are designed to better protect seniors. The American Academy of Family Physicians urges them to choose one — “but do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available,” said AAFP’s Dr. Sarah Nosal.
The Food and Drug Administration recently approved a new choice for people ages 50 and older, the first flu vaccine made with the same mRNA technology that was key to ending the COVID-19 pandemic. One study found Moderna's mFlusiva was 27% more effective against symptomatic illness among 50- to 64-year-olds than a standard shot.
The shot-averse could choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if they're ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria.
COVID-19 shots once were recommended for just about everyone by federal health agencies, but like last year, the FDA has only formally approved them for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk.
Still, the family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and those with other risk factors. Adults 65 and older should get a fall dose and then a second dose six months later, as immunity wanes over time, Nosal said.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a COVID-19 shot for all children ages 6 months to 23 months, and for older kids with high-risk conditions. It also supports vaccination for any child whose parent wishes it.
With millions of shots administered, there’s no evidence that coronavirus vaccination during pregnancy increases the risk of miscarriage or other problems, “so please get the vaccine,” said ACOG’s Dr. Christina Davidson.
Depending on age, people can choose a shot from Moderna, Pfizer, or the only non-mRNA version from Novavax and Sanofi.
Just like with flu vaccines, these shots are better at preventing severe disease than mild cases. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children.
Common side effects for flu and COVID-19 vaccines are mild and temporary, such as sore arms, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches, and mild fever. They occurred somewhat more often with the new mFlusiva than with standard flu shots.
While pediatricians and some clinics offer both flu and coronavirus shots, they're most common in pharmacies.
For COVID-19 shots, states have more pharmacy rules. For example, Walgreens says it offers those shots without a prescription in all but two states, Arizona and Oregon, but can provide doses for children as young as 3 in some states while others have higher age limits.
Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. If you want to choose mFlusiva, the new Moderna flu option, make sure to double check that your insurance covers it.
Flu experts say October is best, although vaccinations will remain available through the fall — just remember it can take two weeks for protection to kick in. COVID-19 cases rose in the late summer and usually do again around the winter holidays. Some experts say it's also OK to time the coronavirus shot a few weeks ahead of an event you wouldn’t want to miss because of illness, like a special trip or get-together.
RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults.
The family physicians recommend a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems.
It’s also recommended during late pregnancy to protect infants born during RSV season. Separately, the pediatricians recommend a vaccine-like medication for those infants whose moms weren't vaccinated and some other high-risk babies.

The doctor at the center of the botched execution of murderer and Satanist Christa Pike is exclusively pictured by the Daily Mail at his isolated family home – less than 24 hours after the horror.
Dr Mark Fowler, 69, came to the door of the house just outside Union City, Tennessee and declined to discuss Pike surviving two syringes of the purportedly lethal injection drug pentobarbital.
’Thank you for coming. I have nothing to say,’ he said from behind the screen door of the four-bedroom property set on 1.5 acres.
Fowler lives 160 miles northwest of the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville where 50-year-old Pike was injected with seven needles on Wednesday night, according to one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey.
She remains alive and is in critical condition at an ‘off-site’ medical facility, which local TV station WSMV has named as Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Pike's case marks the second botched execution in Tennessee this year - both of which were overseen by Fowler.
Fowler was supervising triple-killer Tony Carruthers' execution in May when the death row inmate survived 90 minutes of failed attempts by the medical team to establish an IV connection for the lethal dose.
A complaint against Fowler, filed by Carruthers’ sister, Dr Tonya Hervey, with the Tennessee Department of Health, claimed that 40 minutes into the execution attempt, the doctor took over the search for vein access and announced he was going to set a central line – a large flexible tube inserted into a chest vein.
Dr Mark Fowler, 69, who oversaw the botched execution of murderer and accused satanist Christa Pike in Tennessee was spotted for the first time at his home on Thursday
Christa Gail Pike, now 50, is alive and in critical condition in the hospital after surviving the botched execution
The tube’s needle was pushed into Carruthers’ chest while he was ‘wide awake and groaned in agony,’ the complaint claims.
Dr Hervey also alleges Fowler was unqualified to place the line because he previously admitted in a deposition that he had not performed the procedure for more than a decade.
According to the claim, Carruthers suffered a stroke as a result of the botched execution, leaving him partially paralyzed.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee later called off the execution and gave a one-year reprieve to Carruthers, 58, who was convicted of the 1984 kidnapping and murders of Frederick Tucker, Marcellos Anderson and Anderson’s mother, Delois.
Fowler could face formal disciplinary charges if the health department finds evidence of a violation in its review.
He has previously refused to comment on the complaint on the accusations. But he told NBC, 'Every attempt was made to minimize the defendant’s discomfort in the case at hand.'
According to his LinkedIn profile, Fowler gained his law degree from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville in 1984 and spent three years as a public defender before retraining as a physician in 1996.
Fowler has worked as an ER physician and a family doctor and is reported to hold several medical directorships.

Fowler, who lives in this isolated family home in Union City, is reportedly paid $3,000 to oversee each Tennessee execution
He began as an ER physician at Baptist Memorial Hospital in Covington, Tennessee in 2008. Since November 2012 he has held the role of ‘corporate medical director, director regulatory affairs’ at Interstate Blood Bank, according to his LinkedIn profile.
On Facebook, the doctor describes himself as ‘Right of Center… a writer and avid outdoorsman.’
Fowler also supervised triple-killer Tony Carruthers' execution in May when the death row inmate survived 90 minutes of failed attempts by the medical team to establish an IV connection for the lethal dose
He is reportedly paid $3,000 to oversee each Tennessee execution and was also involved in the controversial execution of Byron Black in August of 2025 – described by the killer’s attorney Kelley Henry as ‘100 percent botched.’
Black reportedly cried out in pain and shouted ‘I can’t do this’ and ‘it hurts so bad’ while repeatedly lifting his head, according to Newsweek. He was declared dead ten minutes later.
Details of Fowler's history of cases have come under renewed scrutiny ever since Pike, who was slated to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years, somehow managed to survive.
President Donald Trump was among those to blast Tennessee officials over the failure to execute her.
'How does that happen?' Trump said on Thursday. 'Should be easy to do. It shouldn't be very difficult.'

Pike sang, groaned and snored during her more than 90 minutes in the death chamber (pictured) at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her Knoxville Job Corps classmate Colleen Slemmer, was taken to a hospital on Wednesday night after surviving a double dose of the drug Tennessee uses to execute prisoners.
It was not immediately clear what went wrong.
Pike's attorneys said the execution team had worked for an hour to administer the lethal drugs as they struggled to locate a vein.
Spivey, one of her attorneys, said he counted at least seven needles in Pike's left arm.
Pike was singing, cackling and blessing those people in the spectators' room after she had received the first dose that should have killed her, her attorney said.
The scene became even more bizarre when, after the second failed dose, Pike started snoring.
Soon after, witnesses were escorted from the area as Pike was rushed to the hospital, according to her attorney.
More than 24 hours later, Pike's attorneys said she was still in critical condition and receiving 'lifesaving care.'
'We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,' Spivey told reporters.
'But we know she is alive right now.'
Pike had been on death row ever since she was convicted over the 1995 murder of her Knoxville Job Corps classmate Colleen Slemmer
The failed execution led Republican Gov. Bill Lee to order a review - calling what happened 'deeply disturbing' and indefinitely postponing Pike’s execution, as well as another one scheduled for later this year.
Meanwhile, Pike's lawyers now want her death sentence to be commuted.
Pike and her boyfriend had both been convicted of the fatal stabbing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer three decades ago.
The killing stoked fears of Satan worship at the time because of a pentagram carved on Slemmer’s body.
Pike, for her part, never disputed that she helped kill Slemmer, but supporters argued her mental illness and allegations of severe sexual abuse should be considered. She was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder shortly after the killing.
'It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,' Pike once said.

After ripping a time of 45.84 in the prelims of the 100 free, all eyes will be on Cameron McEvoy in tonight's final in Baku. Archive photo via Mickael Malaper/ Malaper Photography
October 02nd, 2026 Asia , Europe , International , News , Swimming World Cup Series
The second night of finals from the 2026 World Cup stop in Baku gets underway one hour earlier today, with 10 events on tap and plenty of superstars in action.
This morning, Cameron McEvoy turned heads with an impressive 45.84 clocking in the men’s 100 free, putting him in pole position to complete the sprint double after winning the 50 last night over Egor Kornev .
McEvoy is using the World Cup stops to test out how his training for the 100 free is working after finding vast success in the 50 over the past three years.
The women’s 200 free will be one race to watch with Siobhan Haughey claiming the top seed this morning after an impressive 50 free swim on Thursday, while the men’s 50 breast looks like one of the marquee races of the session with a star-studded field headlined by Qin Haiyang and Caspar Corbeau .
Yu Yiting put on a dominant display in the timed final of the women’s 400 IM, opening up a massive early lead before comfortably winning gold by nearly four seconds in a time of 4:24.09.
Yu went out like a rocket, turning in 57.51 after the first 100, not too far off world record pace, and then she checked in at 2:04.30 at the halfway mark, more than six seconds clear of the rest of the field.
Her gap slowly shrunk a bit on the back half, but it didn’t matter as Yu finished well clear of the field in a time that puts her just shy of the Chinese Record set by Ye Shiwen in 2012 (4:23.33).
Yu also took down her lifetime best of 4:27.81, set in 2024.
Great Britain’s Abbie Wood was the fastest breaststroker in the pool, solidifying her silver medal position on the third discipline before holding off Chang Mohan on the freestyle leg to touch 2nd in 4:27.95.
Chang and Waka Kobori both made big pushes on the last 25 to inch ahead of Ellen Walshe and placed 3rd and 4th, respectively. Chang won bronze in 4:28.76 ahead of Kobori (4:28.97) and Walshe (4:29.13).
Known more for his freestyle and butterfly prowess, Egor Kornev showed that his pure speed and dynamic underwaters translates over to backstroke as well, winning the men’s 50 back final in record fashion.
Kornev blasted out to the early lead at the halfway mark, flipping in 10.86, just one one-hundredth off world record pace, and then used another blazing-fast underwater to solidify his lead off the wall, powering home to touch in a final time of 22.23.
The performance shatters Isaac Cooper ‘s World Cup record of 22.58, set in 2024, and pulled him within 12 one-hundredths of Kliment Kolesnikov ‘s world record of 22.11 set in 2022.
Kornev’s previous best time stood at 22.44, set last December at the Vladimir Salnikov Cip.
Pieter Coetze and Pavel Samusenko , who tied for silver at the 2025 World Championships in the 50 back, incredibly did the exact same thing here, posting matching times of 22.51 to share the second step on the podium yet again.
For Coetze, he obliterated his own African and South African Record of 22.75, set in 2024. When he tied with Samusenko last summer at Worlds, he also broke the African Record.
Kolesnikov was in the field, placing 4th in 22.99.
Siobhan Haughey picked up her 20th career World Cup gold medal in impressive fashion, winning the women’s 200 freestyle in a time of 1:51.08.
Haughey, the former world record holder in the event with her Asian Record time of 1:50.31, assumed the lead by the 100-meter turn and then pulled away from the field on the third 50 (28.18) before gaining more time coming home (28.55).
She swept the 200 free at all three World Cup stops in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and appears well on her way to doing it again in 2026. Last year, Australia’s Mollie O’Callaghan broke Haughey’s world record and swept the event at all three legs of the series.
American Anna Peplowski had a consistently-split race to win silver in 1:52.48, dipping under her previous best of 1:52.54 from the 2025 World Cup in Westmont, while China’s Fan Yaqi sat back in 5th with 25 meters to go, but charged home to snag bronze in 1:53.07. Her countrymate Yan Tiaoshan (1:53.43) and Great Britain’s Freya Colbert (1:53.59) were 4th and 5th.
After an impressive win in the 100 IM last night, former Indiana Hoosier Luke Barr delivered another exceptional swim tonight in the final of the men’s 200 IM, claiming gold in decisive fashion.
Barr, using the phenomenal underwaters he’s developed racing in yards, blasted out to the lead at the first 25 and never looked back, soaring to a time of 1:51.34.
The swim marks a massive lifetime best for Barr, who had previously been 1:54.10 at the 2025 World Cup stop in Westmont. Barr moved from Indiana to train with Coley Stickels last June.
Italian Alberto Razzetti sat third throughout the entirety of the race, lurking behind Canadian Finlay Knox , but made a big push on the last 25 with a 12.93 split to snag silver in 1:52.41, with Knox securing the bronze in 1:52.57.
Razzetti wasn’t too far off the 1:52.05 he produced last December at the SC European Championships en route to silver. His lifetime best stands at 1:50.88, set at the 2024 SC Worlds where he also won silver.
After going two-for-two with gold medals in the 50 back and 100 IM on Night 1, Marrit Steenbergen picked up right where she left off on Day 2.
The Dutch star looked smooth en route to winning gold in the women’s 100 back in dominant fashion, putting up a time of 55.17 to tie Kira Toussaint ‘s national record set in 2019.
The performance marked the second best time of the day for Steenbergen, who went 57.76 in the prelims to lower her previous PB of 58.76. Coming into the meet, her LC best time was faster, sitting at 58.33 from this past summer.
Taylor Ruck , the top seed out of the prelims in 56.82, had a strong showing to win silver in 56.49, setting her second PB of the day. Her swim in the heats improved on her previous mark of 56.90, set at the 2025 World Cup in Toronto.
Turning around on a quick double, Anna Peplowski snagged the bronze medal in a time of 56.97, steadily moving through the field over the course of the race after turning 5th at the 25.
Abbie Wood , also swimming a double after the 200 IM, took 4th in 57.56.
In an incredibly tight race, Qin Haiyang found the magic over the closing meters of the men’s 50 breaststroke, stealing the gold medal away from Michael Houlie on the last stroke.
Houlie used his patented front-end speed to establish a narrow early lead, turning in 11.63 at the 2025, and then coming home, Qin managed to move up alongside before out-touching him by three one-hundredths of a second at the wall.
Qin clocked 25.67 for the victory, while Houlie was 25.70 for silver. Qin is the Asian Record holder with his time of 25.38 from 2024, while Houlie was one one-hundredth shy of his best time, having been 25.69 at the 2024 SC Worlds. They were the only two men sub-26 this morning, with Qin clocking 25.81 and Houlie going 25.95 in the prelims.
Russia’s Kirill Prigoda was right with Houlie and Qin at the turn, giving him a buffer over the rest of the field as he claimed bronze in a time of 25.88. Dutch teammates Caspar Corbeau (26.08) and Koen de Groot (26.15) rounded out the top five.
After winning one silver and one bronze last night, Roos Vanotterdijk completed the medal set by winning gold tonight in the women’s 50 fly, clocking 24.96 to be the sole woman under 25 seconds.
Vanotterdijk was just over a tenth shy of her lifetime best of 24.84, set en route to winning silver at the 2025 SC European Championships.
Sweden’s Sara Junevik , who was only 25th in this event last year at SC Euros in 25.94, claimed silver in a time of 25.15, topping the Russian duo of Arina Surkova (25.21) and Aleksandra Kuznetsova (25.35), who were 3rd and 4th.
Junevik’s personal best time stands at 25.04, set back in 2022.

articles.title_orig: Look up: Saturn is at its brightest this weekend
articles.title_zh: Look up: Saturn is at its brightest this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Saturn is at its biggest and brightest as the ringed planet reaches opposition this weekend.
Opposition happens as Earth passes between Saturn and the Sun, bringing the planet to its closest point to Earth for the year, about 784 million miles (1.26 billion km) away. This minimum distance makes Saturn appear brighter than at any other time this year.
Opposition is a great time to observe Saturn because it rises in the east around sunset, reaches its highest point around midnight, and remains visible through dawn. It will appear as a yellowish point of light in the eastern and southeastern sky.
You do not need a telescope to see Saturn, but even a small telescope can reveal the planet's rings and the brightest couple of its 293 moons. While you are spotting Saturn, look a bit higher for a large grouping of four stars astronomers call the Great Square of Pegasus. Up and to the right is the Circlet (ring) of Pisces. These are asterisms, or recognizable patterns within the more official constellations of Pegasus (the winged horse) and Pisces (the fish).
2026's view is very different from last year's when Earth crossed the plane of Saturn’s rings. Though the ring system spans about 175,000 miles, it is, on average, about 30 feet thick, so it effectively disappears when viewed edge-on. Since opposition in 2025, the rings are tilted 7.5 degrees from our perspective, bringing them back into view.
Saturn will be at opposition on Sunday morning at 8:21 a.m., but with clouds expected this weekend, the best views will be tonight, Friday, Oct. 2. The planet will remain an excellent evening target for much of the month.
Saturn’s last opposition occurred Sept. 21, 2025. Saturn reaches opposition every 378 days, or about two weeks later each year, as Earth catches up with Saturn in its orbit. We'll have similar good opportunities to view Jupiter as it reaches its own opposition on Feb. 11, 2027, followed by Mars on Feb. 19, 2027.
