articles.title_orig: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.title_zh: The world’s 10 most stress-free destinations
articles.content_orig:
Emma is a freelance travel journalist and long-standing contributor to The Telegraph. She is the recipient of several writing awards and has twice been named BGTW Travel Writer of the Year. She has spoken as a travel expert at the Royal Geographical Society, the Frontline Club and National Geographic headquarters in Washington DC and her Scottish lilt can occasionally be heard on the BBC’s From Our Own Correspondent. She can be contacted via Instagram at @emmathomsontravels
Emails. Phone calls. Appointments. Passwords. Protein. Water. Eight hours of sleep. Our lives have become a relentless pursuit of doing – and doing everything better. Even travelling can become a to-do list of bucket-list experiences, country counts and “Instagrammable” moments.
The antidote? The (admittedly laughably named) “stillcation” – a new way of holidaying that pushes back against our culture of constant productivity and self-improvement.
It’s not necessarily yoga at sunrise or a silent meditation retreat, although it can be. More simply, it’s about the absence of agenda. Of stripping life back to its essentials: good food, beautiful views, fresh air and anchoring yourself in the present moment. Instead of seeking destinations that offer the most to do, it asks where offers the best conditions for doing less.
“Man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone” was, according to French philosopher Blaise Pascal, the source of all humanity’s problems. Four centuries later, his observation feels oddly prescient. We are rarely sitting still – even when on holiday.
The constant pressure to optimise our lives can lead to chronic dysregulation of the nervous system, says Jamie Clements, a wellness retreat facilitator and author of the upcoming book The Next Breath . “Stress has become the baseline, and calm feels like the exception.”
Tour operators are catching onto our increasing thirst for deeper ways to unplug. Inghams recently ranked almost 100 European destinations according to their “stillest”, with criteria including walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density and forest cover (Scotland’s Wester Ross, see below, took the top spot).
Black Tomato is designing itineraries centred around themes such as “The Gift of Boredom” and “Sonic Sanctuaries”, with quiet-hour museum slots and low-stimulation dining. We’ve also seen a proliferation of Unplugged detox cabins and AirBnbs offering Wi-Fi and technology-free countryside boltholes.
Slowing down switches our nervous system from a fight-or-flight sympathetic state to a rest-and-digest parasympathetic system that lowers blood pressure and improves concentration by possibly stimulating neurogenesis – the creation of new brain cells.
But don’t assume that a stillcation will immediately evoke a state of inward zen. Like any other holiday – where it can take a week to unwind – the first day or two can feel uncomfortable.
The point of a stillcation isn’t simply that sitting around feels nice. Removing the constant demand for attention – and replacing the thrum of traffic, screens and notifications with wind, water, birdsong and walking – may create the conditions in which both mind and body can begin to really recover.
And the benefits extend beyond our own wellbeing. Several of the qualities that make a destination “still” – low population density, dark skies, forests, clean air, biodiversity and quiet trails – are also qualities that depend on healthy, protected environments.
Perhaps that is the real appeal of the stillcation. It doesn’t ask us to abandon movement, curiosity or adventure. It simply changes the objective. Travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are; less about escaping life and more about inhabiting it. In a culture that has turned even rest into something to optimise, doing nothing might be the most radical itinerary of all.
Lungfuls of salty Cornish coastal air, strolls along the South West Coast Path and its secluded beaches, plus one of the UK’s last remaining temperate rainforests make this the ideal space to slow down.
How to do it: Jamie Clements offers a four-day breathwork retreat at Cabilla in Cornwall from £1,250 per person.
Wester Ross – in the remote north-west highlands of Scotland – is an unspoilt mash of moorlands and mountains that is home to pine martens, otters and the elusive wild cat. Its minimal light pollution creates star-rich dark skies.
How to do it: Wildlife Worldwide offer a six-day The Splendours of Wester Ross tour from £1,295 per person.
Glimpse magic in this Swedish Lapland village that’s probably one of the best places on Earth to see the northern lights (September–April) due to its cloud-free “blue hole”.
How to do it: Arctic Direct offer a three-night Abisko tour from £1,795 per person, including flights and activities.
Creating a wrinkled border between France and Spain, the bird-rich Pyrenees are scarce on people and big on open spaces for mindful hiking, yoga and thermal spas to unwind.
How to do it: Much Better Adventures offer a six-night Hike and Wild Swim in the French Pyrenees tour from £1,688 per person, excluding flights.
Switzerland’s “secret valley” is scattered with lö da ler (wooden cabins with books and reading benches), mindful running trails and forest bathing opportunities, including the Senda Botanica – a narrow path through 30 species of trees.
How to do it: Inntravel offer a seven-night Walking and Wildflowers in the Engadine Valley guided tour from £2,086 per person, excluding flights.
Described as one of the last pristine wilderness areas left on Earth, Yukon has a population of about 48,000 people spread across a territory roughly the size of Spain. It offers an extraordinary sense of space for hiking, wildlife watching, paddling and simply being outdoors.
How to do it: Canadian Sky offer a 10-night In the Footsteps of the Yukon Pioneers self-drive tour from £2,069 per person, including flights.
New Zealand ranks second in the world for peacefulness, behind Iceland. Pick the South Island’s Fiordland, Glenorchy and wild West Coast for vast mountains, sparse settlements and trails where the only itinerary is to walk, breathe and look.
How to do it: Pure Pods has off-grid glass cabins scattered across New Zealand from £240 per night.
Mountain trails, monasteries lit by butter lamps and a deliberately low-volume tourism model make Bhutan in south Asia particularly well suited to a holiday centred on contemplation rather than consumption.
How to do it: Raven Tours offer a nine-day Yoga, Culture and Stillness in the Kingdom of Happiness tour from £2,676 per person based on two sharing.
Nowhere serves up remote stillness quite like Torres del Paine National Park. A raw jostle of glacial lakes, mountains and clear air, it is ideal for forest bathing and restorative walking.
How to do it: Chile Nativo offer a five-day Torres del Paine Wellness Retreat from £1,700 per person from October to April, excluding flights.
One of the world’s least densely populated countries, Namibia in southern Africa is home to the oldest desert in the world, exceptionally dark skies and remarkable wildlife. Don’t miss Sossusvlei, Damaraland and the stark Skeleton Coast.
How to do it: Expert Africa offer a 14-day Discover Namibia self-drive safari from £4,220 per person based on two sharing.

articles.title_orig: How to rule the world: The book review no one asked for
articles.title_zh: How to rule the world: The book review no one asked for
articles.content_orig:
I am not smart enough to rule the world — though, it's important to note that I was planning to. I did not walk into my high school guidance counselor's office, crumple up the state-school brochures, and proclaim I wanted to be a dictator, but I liked having the option. Tragically, this backup plan was crushed when I read Theo Baker’s “How to Rule the World.”
My mother strong-armed this book into my life, proclaiming I would identify with the author.
Like any 19-year-old, I ignored this recommendation, creating a multi-month argument with my parent for no apparent reason. I finally made it around to reading the book between my busy summer schedule of rewatching trashy TV and staring at a wall, only to immediately read that the author I was supposed to be so similar to was a self-described nerd. Thanks, Mom; love you too.
I went into the book with absolutely no context, because I refused to read the jacket as a form of protest. The worst part of the book was… I actually liked it. Not just liked; I loved it to the point I became one of those pretentious people who bring a hard-cover book to appointments, coffee shops, even a tennis match. I was just waiting for someone to ask those magic words, "What are you reading?” What had become of me? The last book I read had watercolor rabbits on the cover. They say drugs are a gateway to a life of disaster; I argue this book set me on a worse track… I was a reader!
You may be asking yourself, “Wow, for a book review I have no clue what this book is actually about.” Well, that's why this article is in the humor section, and why I have not been promoted to culture. I am far too self-centered for ethical journalism. Which, ironically, is what the book is about.
Theo Baker was the student journalist who broke the story that led to Stanford President Marc Tessier-Lavigne's resignation. Baker published “How to Rule the World,” documenting the investigative process that exposed Lavigne's falsified scientific reports and uncovered the toxic symbiotic relationship between Stanford's elite students and Silicon Valley's aggressive venture capitalists.
His investigative journalism earned him the George Polk Award, making him the youngest recipient ever at just 18. I would like to take a moment for that to sink in. He was only a freshman. When I was a freshman, I was just trying to figure out how to do my laundry. I was definitely not cracking the core of our nation's problems with capitalism. I mean, it was on my to-do list, but I just never got around to it.
If, for some reason, you are reading this, Theo Baker, I mean, why wouldn't you be? I'm positive The Miami Student has a national foothold. Just know, the high-achieving STEM parents of the world (my mother) see you as their surrogate successful child when their kid decides to go down the dark path of wanting to be a comedian.
I could go more in-depth on the book's discussion of the intricacies of venture capital in the tech industry and Big Pharma, but I honestly was not smart enough to understand it all and would probably get sued for libel. I will say, to all the young people trying to find their place morally, intellectually, and socially: “How to Rule the World” is an incredibly motivating story urging Gen Z to go past their societal constraints to achieve their goals while striving to create a better, more truthful world. And to President Crawford, don’t worry, I am definitely not clever enough to be an investigative journalist!
Who in the newsroom wants to talk about organic chemistry? Carley would love to.
Mia loves the environment and will do anything to help it flourish. Although, there was this one time...
Cupcake games are awesome... but not for the team that is the cupcake.

articles.title_orig: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000 - ABC News
articles.title_zh: An Ebola treatment center was burned down as the death toll in Congo passes 4,000 - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Congo's Ebola outbreak has resulted in over 4,000 deaths, with authorities struggling to contain the virus
BUNIA, Congo -- Congo's Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people, authorities said, as they struggle to contain what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
The latest figures released by the Health Ministry on Thursday showed that 4,018 people have died among 8,300 cases recorded since the outbreak was declared in eastern Congo on May 15.
Some health workers, meanwhile, gathered at the epicenter in Ituri Province to demand payment for wages owed them. The protesters, who included surveillance team members, waved placards saying, “No money, no data!” and “No payment for months.”
Some of the workers haven't been paid for August and September, said Biongi Beiza, one of the protesters in Bunia, Ituri's capital. “There is no explanation from the administration,” he said.
Congolese authorities did not immediately address the issue. Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
A senior U.N. official said an Ebola-hit displacement camp housing a transit center for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
Creating such transit and treatment centers has been a struggle, requiring money and staff, all of which are in short supply, said Julien Harneis, the U.N. senior Ebola coordinator. "When we lose a center, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment, and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need,” Harneis said.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived in the Netherlands late Thursday on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
“The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country,” MSF said.
At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
One way local authorities have tried to contain the outbreak is through mobile laboratories. In Butembo, an Associated Press journalist watched a medical team operating one such lab near an Ebola treatment center on Thursday.
Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours with the mobile labs, said Lota Kalubi, a doctor at the treatment center.
The labs have also made it easier to get to locations usually difficult to reach, said Michel Ngimba with the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Butembo. “So we can go, if today we have an emergency, for example, in Katwa, we can start up the vehicle, and we can move the lab to Katwa,” said Ngimba.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm about the virus’ rapid spread into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The current outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said.
The number of newly confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hot spots, Africa CDC said on Thursday. While the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others.
Confirmed cases fell from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.
A Congolese politician was beaten to death earlier this week in one of the emerging hot spots after defending government measures to deal with the outbreak, highlighting tensions and mistrust in communities.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach that involved working with local leaders to educate people about the virus, but those efforts face resistance from residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons including how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks and chronic corruption.
Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi in Butembo, Congo, Chinedu Asadu in Abuja, Nigeria, and Mike Corder in the Netherlands contributed.

articles.title_orig: 2031 Women’s World Cup bid update on agenda for FIFA Council meeting
articles.title_zh: 2031 Women’s World Cup bid update on agenda for FIFA Council meeting
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA Council will hear an update on the bid process for the 2031 Women’s World Cup, which is tentatively slated to be held in the U.S., Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, at its Oct. 14 meeting. It will be the first such update since FIFA delayed the vote on awarding the event to the four nations from its Congress this past April to an Extraordinary Congress on Nov. 23.
The joint bid from the four Concacaf nations , submitted last November, is the only one for the 2031 Women’s World Cup. It included 35 prospective host cities: 27 in the U.S., six in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica.
Because of the one-sided nature of the host city agreements for the 2026 men’s World Cup, however, the prospective U.S. host cities refused to agree to specific hosting terms before the 2031 bid was submitted. They are seeking an opportunity to negotiate more favorable terms that would reduce their financial and operational burdens while providing greater revenue opportunities.
It is unknown whether any meaningful discussions have taken place since the conclusion of the men’s World Cup regarding new terms for the 2031 Women’s World Cup. U.S. Soccer is expected to play a role in facilitating those discussions after largely being sidelined in the delivery of the men’s World Cup.
The Women’s World Cup bidding update will also touch on the 2035 Women’s World Cup, for which the U.K. is the lone bidder. Other notable agenda items for the Oct. 14 meeting include a review of President Gianni Infantino’s controversial FIFA Forward Enterprise investment proposal, which was scrapped following massive backlash , as well as reviews of FIFA’s reserves and the financing of its member associations. The agenda also mentions a discussion of the FIFA Peace Prize, which was awarded for the first time in 2025 to President Trump .
The FIFA Council has 37 members, including representatives elected through each of the six regional confederations. U.S. Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone sits on the council as Concacaf’s North American representative.

articles.title_orig: 5 European nations follow U.S. with plans for third-country deportations as EU approves migrant "return hubs"
articles.title_zh: 5 European nations follow U.S. with plans for third-country deportations as EU approves migrant "return hubs"
articles.content_orig:
Five European Union countries are pushing ahead with plans to start deporting asylum seekers whose applications are rejected to third countries outside the bloc, potentially in Africa, after the EU approved new rules this week that clear the way for the practice.
Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands have agreed on a common framework to establish "return hubs" outside the EU to which people who have exhausted their legal options to remain in Europe could be transferred if they cannot be sent back to their own countries of origin.
"When it comes to return hubs, it's progressing very well," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bødskov told reporters Thursday, according to AFP . "We are moving in the right direction."
He previously said Denmark expected "to be ready to transfer the first irregular migrants to a partner country outside the EU within 2027."
Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris told Politico that Greece expects to have a pilot project in place in the first half of next year.
No potential destinations for EU return hubs have been confirmed, although Rwanda has been reported as a possible partner in the project. A Greek government statement on the plans said the hubs would be established in safe third countries, "particularly on the African continent."
The EU itself has presented the idea of return hubs as a potential deterrent to irregular immigration. A discussion paper published by the EU's governing European Council in October 2025 said the hubs could "incentivize voluntary returns," because migrants who fail to comply with a deportation order could face transfer to a hub instead.
It said the policy could also discourage people without a valid asylum claim from making dangerous journeys to Europe.
The rules adopted this week by the EU establish a bloc-wide legal framework for returns and allow member states to conclude bilateral or unilateral agreements with countries outside the bloc, but with stipulations.
Under the rules, "any such agreement or arrangement may only be concluded with a non-EU country that respects international human rights standards and principles of international law, including the principle of non-refoulement ," which guarantees that no individual can be sent back to a country where they would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, punishment or other irreparable harm.
The Trump administration has enthusiastically embraced the use of third-country deportations to remove undocumented migrants from the United States. More than 100 deportees were sent to eight African countries over a 10-day period in August, according to internal U.S. government documents obtained by CBS News .
The deportees were sent to destinations including the African nations of Liberia, Rwanda, Eswatini and Sierra Leone.
Plevris, Greece's migration minister, has praised the Trump administration's approach.
"I am a fan of President Trump," he told Breitbart in August. "But if you ask me what was the best thing he did, it was change the migration policy of the USA, because now we have a new migration policy also in Europe."
Other European governments have experimented with deportations to third nations before, however, with mixed results.
Britain's former Conservative Party government sought to send asylum seekers who arrived through irregular routes to Rwanda to have their claims processed there. The U.K. Supreme Court ruled the scheme unlawful in 2023, before it ever got going, over the risk that refugees could ultimately be returned to countries where they faced persecution.
The following year, the policy was formally abandoned by the new Labour Party government after the Conservatives were voted out of power. The British Home Office said £715 million (almost $950 million) had been spent on the Rwanda program by June 2024, and no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated. Four people traveled voluntarily to Rwanda under the program.
"One lesson may be that European governments should expect litigation, even where the third country looks considerably less controversial than Rwanda," Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory, told CBS News on Friday.
"These policies are often justified as deterrence measures, and that assumes a sufficiently large share of people believe there is a realistic chance they will actually be transferred," Walsh said. "If only a very small proportion can be moved, the deterrent may be much less credible."
"The broader lesson from Rwanda is that externalization is not a shortcut around the difficult parts of migration policy," he said. "It may relocate some of those difficulties geographically, but governments still have to deal with courts, individual rights, administrative capacity, countries that may not cooperate with returns, and substantial costs"
The push for return hubs is part of a broader effort by European nations to tighten their immigration policies amid intense pressure on governments to increase the number of people without a legal right to remain who are actually removed.
Jacob Reynolds, policy director at the Freedom and Sovereignty Initiative Europe, a right-wing think tank based in Brussels, called the EU decision to embrace these hubs a "welcome step towards gaining control of our borders and removing those who have no right to be here."
But he added that "outsourcing the problem of illegal migration to third countries — as the EU has long done — risks avoiding the broader problem: the lack of control over EU countries' borders."
He called for "much more fundamental action" to address "the generous regimes available to asylum seekers in Europe," and said until that happened, "the problem will not be solved."

The World Monuments Fund (WMF), an independent organization, has warned that funding constraints, intensifying climate change, and a lack of access to expertise are putting World Heritage Sites at extreme risk.
The information comes from WMF’s review of 372 nominations submitted by the public from around the globe as research for the upcoming biannual World Monuments Watch (WMW) list, which will be announced in February. According to the findings, eighty-six percent of nominators cited “funding shortages and economic development” as a primary issue, an increase of 6 percent from last year. Simultaneously, 63 percent identified “opportunities to leverage heritage to support local economies through sustainable tourism, job creation, and urban regeneration.”
“This year’s nominations show that the pressures on heritage are intensifying while the resources to protect it are not keeping pace,” Bénédicte de Montlaur, WMF president and CEO, said in a press release. “According to findings in the UNESCO Global Report on Cultural Policies, only one in four countries has the means to safeguard its heritage.”
Sixty-six percent of nominators cited climate hazards as another major concern, and 30 percent said sites were directly threatened by extreme weather events, flooding, storms, drought, and wildfires. Climate impacts are most severe in sub-Saharan Africa, where 86 percent of sites are under threat. At the same time, the need for technical expertise is increasing, yet 35 percent of nominators identified a “severe lack” of local preservation expertise. In Ghana, for instance, the ten shrines of the Asante Traditional Buildings are endangered as traditional stewardship by master craftspeople declines.
Brinda Somaya, an architect and chair of the WMW International Expert Panel, emphasized the urgency of addressing these risks. “Protecting these sites is vital for preserving local memory, fostering economic resilience, and supporting the communities tied to these places,” she said.

articles.title_orig: A Cross-Border Problem: Modeling New World Screwworm’s South American Range
articles.title_zh: A Cross-Border Problem: Modeling New World Screwworm’s South American Range
articles.content_orig:
Traumatic myiasis is about as gross as it gets.
A gravid New World screwworm fly ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) lumbers through the air, looking for the perfect place to deposit her heavy burden of eggs—maybe an open wound or an exposed mucus membrane. Eventually, they’ll hatch out tiny maggots, each sporting a treacherous spiral of backwards-facing spines. These will anchor the maggots as they use razor-sharp mouth hooks to burrow and tear into tender living tissue.
Historically, New World screwworm has been considered a livestock issue, affecting domesticated animals like cattle, sheep, and goats. But a wide range of warm-blooded animals can be hosts—including wildlife, household pets, and even humans.
That’s one takeaway from a recent study, published in August in the Journal of Medical Entomology , that applied a One Health approach to modeling New World screwworm distribution across South America. The team comprised disease experts, data analysts, entomologists, and veterinarians from institutions in Chile, Paraguay, and Venezuela.
“We all knew the fly affects livestock, but as we went through the literature, we came across cases in wildlife, such as maned wolves, giant otters, ocelots, lesser grisons, and wild boars,” says lead author Marlon Mauricio Ardila, a Ph.D. student at Chile’s Universidad de Concepción. “And that’s when you grasp the real problem. Those wild populations are completely outside the reach of any veterinary control, so they act as a reservoir that can keep the cycle going—even when you think you’ve already brought the fly under control in livestock.”
New World screwworm once affected a large swath of the Americas, from the southern United States through central Argentina. A program utilizing the sterile insect technique began in the 1950s and continued through the turn of the century to eradicate the fly in the U.S., Mexico, and central America. But it has returned to Central America in the past couple of years, reaching the U.S. this summer. All the while, populations remained strong in South America. But co-author Leidi Herrera of the Universidad Nacional de Asunción, Paraguay, and the Universidad Central de Venezuela says population data was limited.
“My research into metaxenic diseases and zoonoses … revealed significant gaps in surveillance in our region,” she says. “Although screwworm myiasis has a severe impact on health and the economy in Latin America, studies in South America were scarce.”
Existing models mainly looked at Argentina and Chile plus some nation-level analysis in some other South American countries. Now, the team wanted to model the distribution of New World screwworm for the entire region, with a strong focus on finding environmental conditions that might lead the flies to persist or disperse.
To do this, they used modeling tools along with records of New World screwworm myiasis cases in humans and other warm-blooded animals across nine geographic areas. The data included cases of more than 9,000 New World screwworm larvae, which broke out to about 38% involving human myiasis and nearly 62% involving non-human animals or unspecified myiasis.
This ecological modeling found that temperature and rainfall heavily influence the distribution of New World screwworm in South America—especially winter thermal stress. It turns out screwworm larvae and pupae don’t do well when the temperature dips to its lowest seasonal extreme. They also struggle when the temperature during the day is unstable, which is known to affect how well insects do normal things like fly, mate, and lay eggs.
The models also predict that some places—like the humid lowlands of eastern Paraguay, northeastern Brazil, and parts of the Amazon basin—have exactly what New World screwworm need to thrive: sufficient moisture so their pupae don’t dry out and plenty of opportunities for the flies to find vulnerable (and ostensibly tasty) wounds.
The team used epidemiological records to confirm and extend the models.
Overall, the team say that this problem is one that combines issues of the environment, animal health, and public health—and therefore requires an integrated approach to surveilling and responding to the threat.
“This is a starting point, not the end,” says Ardila. “For now, the paper calls for strengthening surveillance, training producers, and coordinating control across countries—because this is a cross-border problem.”
It also leaves many questions still open: confirming how wildlife act as a reservoir, figuring out the genetic barrier that prevents the flies from taking up areas that seem perfect from a climate perspective, and looking at how other flies that cause myiasis overlap New World screwworm . Herrera says they’re seeking partnerships and funding to design integrated monitoring tools and control strategies.
One thing is certain: It’s work that needs to be done together.

                     performances to Hattiesburg through its 2026-27 Connoisseurs Series. The series opens Oct. 27 at 7:30 p.m. in Marsh Auditorium with “A Centennial Celebration
                     of Miles Davis and John Coltrane.” The year 2026 marks the 100th birthday of the two
                     iconic artists in the world of jazz. The influence of Miles Davis and John Coltrane

                     Quartet with Dr. Sam Bruton on piano, bassist Dr. David Pellow and Nathan Sanders

Haitians remain in the grip of lethal gang violence as it continues to “adapt and expand”, the UN’s top rights official, Volker Türk, said on Friday.
In an update to the Human Rights Council , the High Commissioner welcomed the first Gang Suppression Force operations, mandated by the UN Security Council .
These will help boost security in Haiti “but the Force remains far below the strength needed”, Mr. Türk insisted, in support of its “full, accelerated deployment” with human rights safeguards embedded.
At least 5,700 people have been confirmed killed or injured by gangs – or during operations against them – since 1 January, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR .
Gang members have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped at least 1,000 women and girls. The real figures are likely much higher, Mr. Türk said.
In his update, the High Commissioner for Human Rights also warned that “extortion, looting and destruction of property” are crippling economic activity in Haiti.
The “constant danger” prevents people from reaching schools, hospitals, and essential services, Mr. Türk stressed.
Three hijacked ships have been freed after months in captivity, but five seafarers died during the rescue of one of them, the head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has said.
IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez offered his condolences after the operation to free the HONOUR 25 in Somali waters on 29 September, in which several other crew members were seriously injured.
Mr. Dominguez said seafarers “should not have to lose their lives for the service they provide for the world”, and called for renewed resolve, targeted cooperation and the resources needed to stop piracy in the region.
The HONOUR 25 was one of three vessels released this week, along with the SEAMULL (also known as SIBU 1) and the MT EUREKA, all seized between April and August by pirates and armed robbers.
In total, 44 seafarers were freed and their governments are working to arrange their repatriation. Mr. Dominguez thanked Somalia's Government for its efforts, but noted that 22 seafarers remain captive aboard the ASANA.
He urged Governments to bring new initiatives, such as the proposed Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, to the IMO, and stressed the importance of the EUNAVFOR Aspides and Atalanta operations for maritime security in the region.
An additional 11.7 million women and girls in 28 countries could face food insecurity by the end of the year due to the escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
These crises are driving up food prices and putting a strain on livelihoods and household resources, UN Women said in new analysis published on Friday.
Presenting the findings to journalists in Geneva, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said the estimates are a potential scenario, not a forecast, and that the number is in addition to the 208 million women and girls who were already estimated to be food insecure or malnourished in these countries.
“Experience from past conflicts shows that when food is scarce, women often reduce the amount they eat or skip meals so that children and other family members can eat,” she said.
The greatest numbers of women and girls at risk are in populous countries, while South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen and Palestine face the highest concentration of overlapping vulnerabilities.
UN Women recommends linking food and cash assistance to nutrition, protection, employment and agricultural services. Women should also have access to land, credit and productive resources.
The agency also highlighted the need for better collection of data that shows where food insecurity is worsening and who is eating less, losing income and carrying the heaviest burden of unpaid care work.

articles.title_orig: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.title_zh: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.content_orig:
Gino has proudly served the Tonawanda community from 351 Fries Road since opening his doors in 1983.
Now in his fourth decade of making pizza at his eponymous restaurant in Tonawanda, Gino Pinzone is a part of the old guard who made Buffalo pizza a thing. At seventy years old, he still gets behind the counter of Gino’s Pizza Place at 9 a.m. to make dough, prep sauce, and mentor a new generation of employees.
You’ve been a fixture in the local food scene for decades. Where did that passion for cooking begin?
Everything started back in Sicily. My mother had eleven children, so she worked at home day and night, night and day, constantly cooking for fourteen people. I’m number eight, so I did a lot of helping, making everything you could possibly make at home. I still do it for myself today. I learned everything from her.
Did she teach you to bake?
In those days, we really could not afford meat. Bread was everything. Chinese people use rice. Mexicans use tortilla shells. We were heavy on bread. When it came out of the oven, it was a treat just to put extra virgin olive oil and black pepper on it. That was it.
How did you end up owning a pizzeria?
I went to Buffalo State for Industrial Arts; I was going to be a teacher. But in 1978, my older brother opened a pizzeria and asked me and my brother Frank to work for him. I liked it a lot. I never finished my master's degree in teaching because I was doing okay making pizzas with my brother! I opened my first solo place in November 1983, and here I am today.
What do you love the most?
My employees. Some started as high school students from across the street. They start folding boxes and then, little by little, I teach them how to do a few things here and there. They might go away for college, but they always come back. It’s rewarding. Take care of the employees because the employees will always take care of you. And that’s what they do. I trust them, and they do a great job.
It sounds almost like a family atmosphere .
I get kids coming in who might be a little quiet or shy. Their parents ask if I can hire them, to get them out of their bedrooms and away from the video games. Next thing you know, they’re hopping around and working and loving it. I tell them, “You’re learning a skill.”
It’s not just about making pizzas but also learning how to get around a restaurant. You need to do dishes, you need to cut celery, you need to do this... Even if they graduate and get a degree, they can go anywhere in the world and work in a pizzeria because they know how a kitchen moves.
Many of the restaurant’s Instagram reels feature you. Do you enjoy being in the spotlight?
[Laughs] My son Phil does all that! He puts the camera in my face and says, “Dad, we’re introducing eggplant pizza today.” I always tell him, “Phil, I’m not doing a second take.” Whatever comes out of me, comes out. We did one video recently that had 20,000 viewers. People come in now just because they want to see me and talk to me.
Why have you never expanded to a second location?
I want to be totally responsible for everything that comes out of the place. I do all the prep work. I’m there from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. every day. On Fridays, I’m there until dinner is over. On Sundays, I’m there until the Bills game is over.  Nobody does it like the owner. It’s hard to train somebody to do things the way I do. Nowadays, people open five places and there’s no personal feeling.
And after forty years, most people would be taking it easy. What keeps you coming back every morning?
It’s not the money. It’s the DNA of a pizza guy in me. I see regulars who came in as kids now bringing their own grandkids in and putting them up on my counter. Why would I walk away? It makes it all worthwhile.

articles.title_orig: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.title_zh: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.content_orig:
As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project .
Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas .
At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico.
For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people . They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right.
While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before.
“This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.”
Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county , where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer : its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people.
The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more.
The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.)
To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright.
“This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.”
Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property.
Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality . She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench.
“Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.”
When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property.
Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest.
“You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents.
“We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said.
Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down.
“Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did.
On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again.
San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records.
The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again.
Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property.
When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment . Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene.
About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials.

For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. articles.title_orig: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.title_zh: The Endhó Dam: One of the World’s Least Known Sacrifice Zones
articles.content_orig:
Environmental Law and Climate Policy Insights
Last week, about halfway down the New York Times’ Monday morning newsletter, there was a video titled “ Living Next to Mexico’s Toxic Reservoir .”  I watched it, appalled not only by the dangerous conditions described in the video and accompanying article , but also by the fact that I had never heard of this enormous environmental justice disaster.  I worried that if I—someone who inevitably spends some part of everyday thinking about environmental injustices—was previously unaware that over 20,000 people have been forced to live around a toxic reservoir for approximately five decades , then it was unlikely that these communities had been receiving much, if any, attention and support from environmental organizations outside of the region.  It turns out that, unfortunately, my concern was well-founded.  In 2023, Judges for the Society of Environmental Journalists’ 22nd Annual Awards for Reporting on the Environment awarded “ Los Olvidados de Hidalgo ” [English transcript here ]—a N+ Focus feature story about the Endhó Dam—third place, in part because of how “shockingly unknown” the story was.
The Endhó Dam was built in the 1950s as a freshwater reservoir, and for about 20 years, it served as such.  There was plenty of clean water to irrigate the crops in the otherwise arid Mezquital Valley, and the dam provided locals with an enjoyable and clean natural environment .  In the 1970s, however, as the population of Mexico City continued to grow, federal officials decided to begin diverting the capital’s storm runoff and wastewater into the dam.  This means that for the past 50 years, all of the wastewater from a metropolitan area of around 20 million people has been dumped into the Endhó Dam.  Every year, the dam receives around 326 million cubic meters of largely untreated wastewater—that’s enough wastewater to fill over 130,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Approximately 60% of the wastewater does pass through a treatment plant, but before the treated water can make it to the reservoir, it mixes with discharge and waste from a nearby oil refinery, thermopower plant, and the rest of the massive industrial corridor that surrounds the dam.  The result is an environmental and public health nightmare, referred to by locals as “ Mexico’s toilet bowl ,” and “the world’s largest cesspool.”
Yury Uribe, a lifelong resident of the region and activist with El Movimiento Social por la Tierra, has been organizing her community in an attempt to get the Mexican government to recognize the Endhó Dam as an environmental emergency, but through no fault of her own, she has seen little success.  Although the area was declared an ecological restoration zone in 2024, the declaration did not allocate any funding to cleaning up the area.  Accordingly, Endhó Dam residents continue to suffer from seemingly endless environmental and health problems.  Cancer rates in the area tripled between 2007­–2018, and today,
communities surrounding the dam report rates of cancer and kidney failures that are sometimes double the national average ; the dam contaminates the surrounding towns’ wells —the main source of drinking water for those towns’ residents; and the hyacinth that grows on top of the dam has become a breeding ground for mosquitos , endangering locals’ livestock and forcing residents to “ lock themselves inside ” every evening.  Emiliano Rodríguez Mega, a long-time science reporter covering Latin America and the NYT reporter who covered this story, said that even he “ had never quite seen something like the Endhó Dam .”
The big question that normally follows learning about an injustice like this is, “how is this allowed to happen?”  Unfortunately, the answer this time is the same as it almost always is:  some communities—low-income, marginalized communities—are seen as expendable.  As explained by the legendary environmental justice advocates Dr. Robert Bullard and Beverly Wright, the people and communities who are viewed as being expendable suffer from having “ the wrong complexion for protection .”
Areas like the Endhó Dam are often referred to as “ sacrifice zones ” because “the health and safety of people in these communities is being effectively sacrificed for the economic gains and prosperity of others.”  In this instance, the low-income farming communities living around the dam ( a substantial percentage of whom are Indigenous , primarily from the Otomí Nation ) are being sacrificed to protect Mexico City from flooding and to keep the profitable agricultural area surrounding the Tula River rich with nutrients.  Similar cases of environmental injustice and racism exist around the world:  the risk of cancer to the primarily Black residents of “Cancer Alley” in Louisiana is over 50 times higher than the national average; 95% of children in Kabwe, Zambia , largely from poor families, have dangerously elevated levels of lead in their blood caused by the nearby lead mining; nearly every Aamjiwnaang First Nation household living in Canada’s “Chemical Valley” suffers from high rates of miscarriages, asthma, and cancer.  The examples, unfortunately, abound.  Recognizing that these areas “illustrat[e] egregious human rights violations, particularly of poor, vulnerable and marginalized communities,” former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment, David Boyd, described sacrifice zones as “ the worst imaginable dereliction of a State’s obligation to respect, protect, and fulfil[l] the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.”
How do we finally rid the world of a system in which, as Naomi Klein put it in This Changes Everything , “poisoning [whole subsets of humanity] in the name of progress [is] somehow acceptable”?  Like most things worth doing, it’s somewhat complicated.  But as the Climate Justice Alliance—an alliance of over 100 frontline communities in the climate justice movement— has noted , it is critically necessary not only because everyone has a right to drink clean water and breathe clean air, but also because “[o]ur society cannot build a more just and healthy economy if communities continue to be seen as expendable.”  Eliminating sacrifice zones can be distilled into a three-stage process:  (1) prioritize protecting the communities living in sacrifice zones from further harm; (2) allocate resources to repairing the harm that has already been done and passing strong regulations; and (3) invest in the communities that have historically been viewed as expendable, and ensure that they have power over their own futures.  Let’s get to work.

October 2nd, 2026 by Justin Melillo
The Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series continues this Saturday, October 3rd, featuring 32 of the best sim racers around the globe. Next up, the competition heads to Suzuka Circuit in Japan for the third round of the five-round season.
Another two names were added to the winner’s list after Silverstone last week in Diogo Pinto and Dayne Warren. Once again, two drivers from the Red Bull / Verstappen camp and the Coanda camp, respectively, as they joined Florian Lebigre and Charlie Collins who won in the opening round. Will it be another split at Suzuka, or can one team take full control?
Live streaming of the events will begin on Saturday at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .
Diogo Pinto, Dayne Warren score victories at Silverstone | Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship
The biggest action from Silverstone came in qualifying and in the battle for eighth in the Sprint. Diogo Pinto just took the pole position over Alejandro Sánchez, which allowed for him to take the lead on the start and go on to win the Sprint. Behind that, Cooper Webster qualified in eighth, and was on track to finish there, but managed to pass Dayne Warren for seventh before the checkers. That wound up putting Warren in first for the Main, and Warren would go on to win after 30 minutes.
There have been seven prior seasons of the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship Series, but never in those previous 64 races has there been a trip to Japan to take on the twists and turns of Suzuka International Racing Course.
One of the world’s truly great race tracks, Suzuka has been the home of the Japanese Grand Prix since the 1980s and its flowing layout regularly puts the circuit at or near the top of the list of most Formula One drivers’ favorites. As if that weren’t enough, Suzuka boats three different configurations – Suzuka East, Suzuka West and Suzuka Full, the latter two featuring a rare figure eight layout where the back straightaway crosses the front section track on an overpass.
Designed by noted circuit architect John Hugenholtz (who also designed the original Zandvoort circuit), Suzuka opened in 1962 and served primarily as a test track for Honda and as the site of sports car racing including the Suzuka 1000K and the 8 Hours of Suzuka and MotoGP motorcycle events. Suzuka was nominated to stage the Japanese Grand Prix in 1987 and has often been the site of the Formula One season finale. As such, Suzuka has been the decisive event in some of the closest battles for the World Championship of Drivers and has witnessed a number of controversial incidents, including clashes between Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost. Suzuka also hosted non-championship NASCAR races in 1996 and ’97.
In addition to its signature crossover layout, Suzuka features a number of notable challenges including a testing series of esses, the multi-apex Spoon Curve and dauntingly fast 130R corner. The race track also serves as the foundation for a major sports and entertainment facility including an amusement park whose giant Ferris Wheel is prominent in photographs and television images of the circuit.
After Suzuka, the Porsche Esports Supercup World Championship heads to the Autódromo José Carlos Pace, or Interlagos for short, for the fourth round of the season. The events are scheduled for Saturday, October 10th, and will be live starting at 19:00 GMT (3:00 p.m. ET) via Porsche’s channels on YouTube and Twitch .

articles.content_orig:
Lydia Wilhelm 02 October 2026
Would it really be a prospective student visit without a free t-shirt? If you see a student walking backwards across campus giving a Taylor tour, you’re bound to see some visitors with classic Taylor purple t-shirts hanging over their arms. However, you might not know that this common prospective student gift is creating uncommon change in the lives of Guatemalan families through Taylor’s partnership with World Orphans .
World Orphans is a non-profit organization with a vision of relational healing and financial independence for families who have been separated due to poverty or abuse. One of the ministry arms within the organization is the World Orphans Market , an economic empowerment program. This program equips women with sewing skills, and these women are then employed as artisans to return to them the dignity of meaningful work and financial freedom. All of World Orphans’ work is grounded in a Christ-centered philosophy of human worth: everyone is created with intrinsic dignity and with a God-given purpose. Additionally, World Orphans works through local churches, ensuring that these women are supported by Christ-centered communities as they work their way out of poverty and towards better lives for their families.
Like so many Taylor stories, Taylor’s journey to partnering with World Orphans is a story of community. When the Admissions team connected with World Orphans, they saw an opportunity—an opportunity for Taylor as an organization to model the same mission it seeks to foster in its student body. Taylor always has a need for t-shirts—particularly in Admissions. Here, Taylor’s tangible need for shirts meets these Guatemalan women’s tangible need for living-wage work, creating a true, mutually beneficial partnership.
As the Admissions team collaborated with World Orphans’ Guatemalan team, they encountered some community connections that made one thing clear—God had already been opening doors for this partnership. One of these connections was Lily Sachsenmeier ’26, who finished her Orphaned & Vulnerable Children degree interning at World Orphans in Guatemala, where "a highlight was getting to talk with social workers at World Orphans who support local families, empowering parents with education and resources to care for their children. I was really moved by the personal experiences they shared and by their passion for their work."
During her time in Guatemala, Sachsenmeier also had the opportunity to meet some of the artisans making the t-shirts for Taylor Admissions, bringing this community story full circle.
Reflecting on Taylor’s choosing World Orphans to supply their next batch of Admissions t-shirts, Sachsenmeier said, "I’m deeply touched that Taylor is partnering with World Orphans. As a student, I got many free t-shirts for events and programs, and I’m so glad that Taylor is being intentional about where they source some of these t-shirts. I’m incredibly proud that Taylor is investing in t-shirts made by these women in Guatemala as part of World Orphans’ economic empowerment program!"
At Taylor, a t-shirt is so much more than a clothing item—it’s a walking billboard for who we are. It says, "I believe in what goes on here." Now, Taylor purple has additional purpose. These t-shirts are a physical manifestation of our mission to "minister Christ’s redemptive love, grace, and truth to a world in need." They are a reminder of a God who opens doors. And a reminder of what a true partnership can look like.

articles.title_orig: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.title_zh: McMinnville siblings earn karate medals around the world
articles.content_orig:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV) - Logan and Kenzie Mendonca, a brother and sister from McMinnville, are competing in karate tournaments around the world.
“We are more stressed watching each other fight than when we are competing ourselves,” Kenzie said.
The siblings have traveled to multiple countries to compete.
“Canada, Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Paraguay, Costa Rica,” Logan said.
“I think Africa, just to make one,” Logan said, referring to places they haven’t competed.
Logan and Kenzie recently returned from Guadalajara, Mexico, with Youth League Karate gold medals. Their medals hang in the family dojo, the Mendonca Academy of Martial Arts in McMinnville.
“It’s a place of calm. I come in here and my problems are outside,” Logan said.
The siblings have competed in karate since they were three years old. Their father, Tony, leads their training routine.
“You learn time management, you learn how to get your things done because the dojo isn’t something that you can skip. It is a mandatory part of your routine,” Kenzie said.
“Just traveling and seeing crazy stuff but also winning and losing together is something really special to me,” Logan said.
Logan and Kenzie competed at the Junior Pan American Karate Championships in San Jose, Costa Rica. Logan won the Junior Male title in his fifth appearance at the event.
“I went bronze, silver, silver, then I took fifth and this year I won, so this year was my first year winning, pulling it out. It was my third year in the finals,” Logan said.
Logan is ranked No. 1 in the U.S. and is a senior at McMinnville High School. Kenzie, a sophomore, won Pan American Cadet Female silver for a third straight year.
“I think the most-cocky part of it for me is being in three finals before Logan,” Kenzie said.
“Yeah, I mean her record is better than mine,” Logan said.
“On paper if you look at like our ages my stuff looks cooler than his,” Kenzie said. “Because I’m better earlier.”
Both Logan and Kenzie were named team captains for the United States. They will next compete at the Junior World Championships in Poland.
“He’s Spiderman but when he comes home, he’s Peter Parker,” Kenzie said.
Logan is a National Merit Scholar semifinalist with aspirations of attending college in France to study physics.
“Right now Peter Parker has national merit, but nobody knows he’s Spiderman and nobody cares,” Kenzie said.
Logan and Kenzie will miss about nine days of school for the trip to Poland. They are completing tests during lunch breaks and will bring homework with them.

articles.title_orig: Apple is reportedly building a smart home camera that won't record video footage of you or anyone else
articles.title_zh: Apple is reportedly building a smart home camera that won't record video footage of you or anyone else
articles.content_orig:
The device will apparently use AI to analyze activity in your home without actually filming it.
After finally making Siri a half-decent assistant in this year's round of major OS updates, it looks like the smart home is going to Apple's big area of focus in the coming months. Reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman revealed earlier this week that the company's long-awaited home hub could arrive later in October, and in the debut episode of his new Power On podcast, he predicted that a security camera may follow. But unlike its many soon-to-be rivals, this one somewhat bizarrely won't actually record video.
As well as the home hub device, which will be the centrepiece of the whole Siri-led smart home push, Gurman claims that Apple will also launch more powerful versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV, which will both support the new Siri AI ecosystem. But the camera is arguably more interesting, as much for what it can't do as what it can.
The Bloomberg reporter says the camera device is a companion product to Apple's also as-yet unannounced smart home display, which the company is referring to internally as J490. These small cameras can be installed around your home and will apparently be cylindrical, resembling chapstick. Gurman says they will have a very low frame rate and crucially won't actually offer video recording as a feature.
What's the point of a camera that doesn't capture moving images, you may ask? Apple appears to be mindful of the growing and very reasonable concerns about over-surveillance and what happens with that data, and so the sensor will instead use AI to analyze movement in your home. It's not clear if you'll be able to pull still images from it, but it will be able to do facial recognition.
If the camera identifies someone walking into a room, it can notify you of whether you know that person or not, but you'll only receive text descriptions. As Gurman points out, a total lack of video footage probably won't be particularly helpful to the police in the event that someone breaks into your home, but the added layer of privacy would definitely make Apple's camera stand out in a crowded market.
Gurman added that the security camera will use "a very similar technology to what they're going to be using for the AirPods with cameras," which leaked over the summer. Based on code buried in an early build of macOS Tahoe 26.7, these AirPods will each have their own tiny embedded cameras that take extremely low resolution RGB still images that can be analyzed using Visual Intelligence. In the wake of Meta's "pervert glasses" fallout, Apple's camera-equipped AirPods reportedly won't be able to take pictures or record video.

articles.title_orig: Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Among Kids and Teens—and It's Not the Same Disease Adults Get
articles.title_zh: Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Among Kids and Teens—and It's Not the Same Disease Adults Get
articles.content_orig:
Jo Henderson was 17 when she was diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer . It came after months of symptoms — stomach pain, bloating, constipation — and months of testing.
“I was expecting a gluten allergy, lactose intolerance,” said Henderson, now 18, of Seekonk, Massachusetts. “Literally anything but cancer.”
Colorectal cancer in people younger than 20 is exceptionally rare: People like Henderson are about one in a million , and account for fewer than 100 cases per year in the United States. But a new study found that most cases of colorectal cancer in kids and teenagers are aggressive, and often diagnosed at advanced stages.
The findings show that “the adolescent and the youngest of the young adults are at particular risk for bad outcomes and are a unique and vulnerable population even compared to people in their 30s and 40s,” said Dr. Danielle Cameron, the director of pediatric surgical oncology at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute in Boston, who worked on the study.
“They are at higher risks for more aggressive types of colorectal cancers and more opportunities for diagnostic delays,” she said.
Cameron stressed that cases in adolescents and very young adults are “still very, very rare.” But anecdotally, experts say they are seeing rates begin to tick up.
Worldwide, rates of colorectal cancer are rising among people in their 20s and 30s. A person born in the 1990s is four times more likely to be diagnosed with colorectal cancer before age 50 than people born in the 1960s were.
Previous research has focused on colorectal cancer in adults under 50 . Cameron and her team went younger, focusing on people under 21.
The team identified 84 adolescents, with a median age of 16, in the United States who’d been diagnosed with colorectal cancer from 2012 through 2023. (Henderson was not a part of the study and Cameron was not her doctor.) The research will be presented at the American Academy of Pediatrics’ national conference in San Diego on Saturday. It has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Most of the young people in the study, 80%, weren’t diagnosed until their cancer had reached Stage 3 or Stage 4, which means the cancer has spread. That tracks with Henderson’s diagnosis: By the time her cancer was found, it had spread to her ovaries.
Once a cancer has spread, it’s much more difficult to treat — in the study, about 37% of the patients’ cancer returned and 45% of the patients died.
Diagnosing colorectal cancer in adolescents can be challenging. They’re decades away from colonoscopies to screen for the disease, and, according to Cameron, “the symptoms they are presenting with are vague.”
In the study, about 74% of people reported back or abdominal pain , and about 45% reported changes in bowel habits. A similar portion of people reported unexplained weight loss and about 32% had rectal bleeding.
“There are a lot more common things that cause those symptoms,” said Dr. Tara Henderson, chair of the department of pediatrics at the Yale School of Medicine, who was not involved in the research. (Tara and Jo Henderson are not related.)
Dr. Christopher Lieu, co-director of gastrointestinal medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, Colorado, said that not every child or teenager who loses weight or has abdominal pain should get a colonoscopy, “but taking symptoms seriously is important.”
If a doctor has ruled out more common issues such as irritable bowel syndrome and things aren’t improving in the short term, doctors should consider ruling out colorectal cancer, said Lieu, who wasn’t involved with the research.
“If it is colorectal cancer, the more we can catch these cases at early stages of disease, the better outcomes will be,” he said.
And then there’s “the million-dollar question,” as Cameron calls it: What’s causing the rise in colorectal cancer in young people?
She suspects that it likely has to do with DNA changes brought on by environmental exposures during childhood.
Dr. Kimmie Ng, the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, said that the rise in ultraprocessed food could be playing a role. Ng, who is Jo Henderson’s oncologist, noted that her previous research found that women who ate more ultraprocessed foods had a higher risk of colon polyps that can be precursors to cancer. Studies looking at whether microplastics could play a role are ongoing, she said.
A common risk factor for colorectal cancer is having a first- or second-degree relative — a parent, sibling, grandparent, aunt or uncle — who’d had the disease. But that was only the case for 20% of the people in the study.
However, “despite there being no family history, they may still have a genetic predisposition,” said Tara Henderson.
About half of the patients in the study underwent genetic testing, which revealed a handful of genetic mutations that can raise the risk of cancer. These mutations aren’t necessarily inherited; instead they can be caused by certain exposures, or simply by chance.
“It really does suggest that some of the exposures that are occurring early in life are playing a role in early-onset colorectal cancer,” Lieu said.
After her diagnosis, Jo Henderson launched into treatment. In December, she had a portion of her colon removed, as well as both of her ovaries, before undergoing five months of chemotherapy. She’s on hormone replacement medicine and will need annual colonoscopies moving forward.
A colonoscopy in August showed no signs of cancer. It was just four days before she was due to move away to college. She’s now a freshman in the Powers College of Business at Clemson University.
