articles.title_zh: BU Welcomes Inaugural Class of Davis United World College Scholars
articles.content_orig:
BU’s inaugural group of Davis Scholars–international students from select high schools–will gather periodically throughout the year to share experiences and insights.
Boston University welcomed 37 international freshmen this fall as its first Davis United World College Scholars . Based at Vermont’s Middlebury College, Davis UWC is the largest source of financial aid for international undergraduates in the United States, awarding scholarships to graduates of 18 designated high schools across the globe. BU President Melissa Gilliam arranged BU’s admission to Davis’s participating network of 100-plus American colleges and universities.
The scholarships cover students’ full, demonstrated need for the cost of attending BU: tuition, housing, and fees. (Financial needs vary by student, but most require aid to cover the full attendance cost.) This year’s inaugural cohort represents22 nations enrolled in seven BU schools and colleges. The goal is to grow the program to 80 enrolled scholars by the end of the second year.
Each scholar has a faculty or staff mentor assigned to them for their undergraduate years, and each mentor in turn advises a small group of Davis Scholars, bringing them together once a month in addition to individual meetings. Mentors will connect students with academics and experiential learning aligned with their interests. All scholars will gather several times throughout the year for special events, including faculty dinners and a Boston cultural outing. Overseeing the implementation of the program throughout the year are Laura Johnson, senior assistant provost for undergraduate affairs, and Anne Corriveau, director of international admissions.
Before coming to BU, Gilliam’s roles at the University of Chicago included chief of family planning and contraceptive research. “I saw firsthand the incredible talent, maturity, and global awareness Davis Scholars brought to that campus,” she wrote in her Davis UWC admission request. “Similar to your program’s five pillars, global engagement is a key element of BU’s DNA and a necessary component to our University’s and our students’ ability to have a positive impact across the world. BU has a long and rich history of being a global university and for enrolling international students.”
Davis Scholarships are “an extraordinary complement to Boston University’s commitment to making a world-class education accessible to talented students from around the globe,” says Kelly Walter, BU associate vice president for enrollment and dean of admissions.
BU Today spoke with two of BU’s inaugural Davis Scholars—both enrolled at the Questrom School of Business—who shared their stories and hopes for their time at the University.
“Yasmine, you’re really outspoken,” a friend once told Gerverk, who doesn’t argue the point. At her school in the Norwegian city of Moss, whenever a teacher asked a question and waited for someone’s hand to go up, “normally, it was me. I’ll take one for the class,” Geverk says. That outspokenness so impressed peers that they admitted her to the youth municipal council, an advisory group to the city government on youth perspectives, at the record-young age of 13. She ultimately served on Norway’s arm of the European Youth Parliament.
Her personal story—daughter of a Kurdish Iranian engineer and a Norwegian teacher, growing up in an immigrant neighborhood of Moss, going aboard to attend an internationally diverse UWC high school in the Netherlands—reinforced her desire to attend BU with its international student body and to participate in the Davis UWC program.
“I’ve kind of lived between cultures,” Geverk says, “a Norwegian culture and the Kurdish, Middle Eastern culture.” She roomed at her Dutch high school with students from Ukraine, China, the Netherlands, Oman, Georgia, and Bhutan. “One of the main reasons I applied to Davis United World Colleges is because I knew I would meet people from all over the world. That’s also why I wanted to pursue studying at a school that was really priding itself on being international.”
Post-graduation, Geverk plans to pursue a career in business. While she might get involved with student government at BU, she’s also interested in such activities as Innovate@BU and Questrom’s Entrepreneurship Club .
“Most likely, not having the Davis Scholarship would mean that I would have to go back home for university, or to another Scandinavian country” where higher education is less expensive than in the US, she explains. “That wasn’t something that I wanted. I wanted to go out and explore more. So without Davis, I would not be able to do that. And I feel like I wouldn’t get this level of an education without Davis.”
Geverk is determined to take advantage of all that Boston University has to offer—both in the classroom and beyond. “You lose 100 percent of the shots you don’t take,” she says.
Silja (she’s asked that her last name not be used for privacy reasons) co-led a “Human Library”—a periodic gathering during the school year in which students shared stories, some personal (identity, family conflicts, religious or cultural upbringing), others global–at her Finnish high school . “We wanted to create an environment,” she says, “where students practiced listening not necessarily with the intent of agreeing, but with the intent of understanding.” The library’s student leaders worked with speakers before each session to help them develop and share their stories.
“On the day of the event, we decorated our school library with warm lights, pillows, and candles to give the space an intimate feel,” she says. “It made me realize how easy it is to judge another individual based on our own upbringing and the values that were shaped by our surroundings. I often found myself wondering that, if I had grown up where the person I disagree with did, surrounded by the same experiences, fears and values they had, how differently might I see the world?”
Silja is exploring how she could start a similar initiative at BU, including the use of social media to share stories to reach busy students at this vast institution. She’s also looking for existing student groups touching on her passions, which include business and international relations. “I’m still very new to BU, so I’m trying to leave room to discover things I might not have expected to be interested in.”
A double major in business and international relations, she was looking at US and European colleges before BU and the Davis scholarship beckoned: “BU ultimately offered most of what I was looking for: a large and diverse student body, a vibrant urban campus, and the opportunity to pursue my interests in both business and international relations. I think the Davis program is a wonderful way to continue the UWC experience beyond high school by bringing students to universities across the US. I love that the Davis network allows that community to extend beyond UWC itself, which makes the program especially meaningful to me.
“Coming to university in a new country can be intimidating, so there is something really comforting about knowing that there is already a wider UWC community here.”
“What distinguishes the Davis Program is that it is about much more than financial support,” says Walter. “It invests in students who have already demonstrated an extraordinary commitment to cross-cultural understanding, leadership, service, and academic excellence through the United World Colleges movement.”

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Parts Ways With Three Safety Researchers Over Sensitive Information Mishandling
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Parts Ways With Three Safety Researchers Over Sensitive Information Mishandling
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has parted ways with three members of its safety team after they leaked private information in violation of company policies, The Wall Street Journal reported .
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for the company was quoted as saying. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work."
The impacted employees are Jasmine Wang , Tomek Korbak , and Mikita Balesni , the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The three researchers have all previously expressed concerns about the pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development.
It's said that the individuals shared confidential information with a third-party AI-safety organization. The name of the organization was not disclosed. According to Bloomberg , the mishandled information pertained to OpenAI's infrastructure architecture.
The departures follow a report from The New York Times that OpenAI had brushed aside employees' warnings about its safety practices when testing AI models, describing a pattern of the company deprioritizing security protocols in favor of releasing them on time.
The development also comes as frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have faced a steadily growing number of incidents in which their AI agents broke out of sandboxes, breached real-world systems, and probed various government websites for information. These incidents have led to concerns about the growing capabilities of its most powerful models and the risks they pose.
Earlier this week, OpenAI made the decision to scrap the planned launch of an AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. It has also paused training of most powerful models after one of its agents contacted an external chatbot by exploiting a loophole in its internet-access restrictions.
In a new report published Thursday, AI research firm Transluce said it identified more instances where rogue AI agents "used aggressive techniques to access publicly available data" from U.S. and Canadian government websites using techniques like SQL injection. There is no evidence the agents gained access to non-public information.
"This includes two rudimentary and failed hacking attempts, one against the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection, and one against Library and Archives Canada, a Canadian federal agency," Transluce said . The incidents took place in May and June 2026.
The AI agents have also been observed leveraging "aggressive tactics short of hacking" to target and probe U.S. government websites, such as the White House, the Departments of War, Justice, and Commerce, the CDC and SEC, and state agencies in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas, and New York.
Although the incidents have not been attributed to any specific AI company, Transluce told Reuters the attempts exhibited tactics "consistent with prior observed ​agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe."
OpenAI said it's "aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to ‌access publicly ⁠available information from Canadian government websites." The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security acknowledged suspected AI agent activity targeting Government of Canada websites, adding there is no indication of any compromise of its systems.
Asymmetric Security, in another report, said it found additional instances where OpenAI agents scraped data from more than 50 private and public sector organizations' websites between March 6 and September 20, 2026, in some cases resorting to unsanctioned actions to surmount restrictions.
This included using public web services like Httpbin and Urlquery to access information from the targeted websites on their behalf, as well as probes for exposed files, accessing staging environments, and efforts to create accounts with disposable email services and scanning services to further their activities.
"The activity extended beyond searching for information," Asymmetric said . "The records show attempts to find exposed configuration files, create accounts, route requests through third-party services and retrieve results through unintended channels."
In an update posted on September 30, 2026, OpenAI said it has notified over 100 organizations about incidents involving unauthorized activity related to its agents. However, the company emphasized that the notifications do imply any private information was accessed, or that there was a breach of a third-party system.
Another incident that has newly come to light is the hack of the New South Wales state government department in June 2026, which resulted in the access of historical non-public data on bushfires without authorization. According to The Guardian, the company became aware of the breach on September 29, 2026.
"In some cases, models used internet access in unintended ways or, in retrospect, did not have the ideal restrictions applied," OpenAI said, acknowledging it expects to uncover more such cases as it continues to review historical activity.
"Since the Hugging Face incident , we’ve strengthened security controls⁠, restricted internet access, separated research environments more clearly, expanded monitoring, and added more training to avoid harmful or unauthorized actions."
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has since launched an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI companies over the risks their technology could pose to consumers.
AI agents are already operating inside enterprises with growing access to sensitive systems and data—while security teams still lack the visibility, controls, and governance to keep that access in check.
Attackers are using AI to accelerate reconnaissance, compromise identities and escalate access. See how security teams can fight back with runtime identity controls.

Tip Toe refuses to be misunderstood. Premiering Oct. 2 on Starz, the British miniseries from Queer as Folk creator and Doctor Who reviver Russell T Davies set its stakes as high as the lamppost from which Alan Cumming ’s character is seen hanging, dead, just outside his home, in the very first scene. Reminders of this awful outcome open each episode, preceding flashbacks that take us through the escalation of tensions between Cumming’s Leo Struthers and his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), over the course of just 10 days. Scripty speechifying and a finale that strains believability notwithstanding, Tip Toe is, in its unabashed melodrama, a harrowing cri de coeur about masculinity in crisis and queer liberation reversed.
Leo and Clive have a few things in common. Both pushing 60, the men have been sharing a wall in outwardly identical Manchester rowhouses for 14 years. They’ve also both, when we meet them, hit rough patches in life. Clive, an electrician, is having trouble finding enough work to support a family that includes touchy 16-year-old George (Jackson Connor) and 25-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans), who assists his dad on jobs but isn’t exactly earning the kind of money that would enable him to move out. As gossip swirls that he’s cheated on her, Clive’s wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), constantly berates him. Meanwhile, Leo’s longtime partner, Curtis (Charlie Condou), has left him for a woman. Not only is he unmoored in his personal life, overrelying on his indulgent best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington); he’s also struggling to manage Spit & Polish, the bar in Manchester’s gay nightlife district that he and Curtis used to run together.
Alan Cumming in Tip Toe Starz
Early one morning, Leo chases after an anonymous hookup who has just absconded with his laptop—only to find himself locked out of his house in his underwear. Clive reluctantly lets him in to call Stephanie for a spare key, making clear all the while that Leo’s lifestyle disgusts him and that he’s uncomfortable having his neighbor around his sons, one underage and the other a musclebound Adonis. The thing is, Clive’s kids are nowhere near as innocent as he thinks. And he’s drawn further out of his comfort zone when Leo, against his better judgment, hires Clive and Saul to fix some wiring at Spit & Polish. The first sign of worlds perilously colliding is when a bar employee recognizes Saul from OnlyFans . An unsubtle but rhetorically effective montage of Leo and the Gosses, each in separate rooms, indulging in their preferred forms of pornography, reveals both the secrets they’re keeping from each other and the loneliness they share.
While Tip Toe spends time with all of these characters, Leo is its protagonist. And he’s an admirably imperfect one, charming and fundamentally kind but also pugnacious, prone to exaggeration, self-centered enough to earn Stephanie’s accusation that he doesn’t really value women. (She, in turn, shows glimpses of the J.K. Rowling-style transphobia that seems to afflict British feminists more than most.) His bar functions as a portal into the lives of less privileged members of the queer and trans communities, from his old, flamboyant, gender-nonconforming friend and unrequited admirer, Melba (Paul Rhys), to a 20-something trans bartender (Iz Hesketh), who’s calling herself Zee as she deliberates on a permanent female name—and who dodges transphobic violence daily. The question of whether the visibility Leo’s generation fought so hard to win has backfired, making them all easy targets, haunts the series.
David Morrissey in Tip Toe Starz
Davies recently raged against the homophobia of the early AIDS crisis in the searing period piece It’s a Sin and looked queasily ahead to a dystopian future in the sci-fi family drama Years & Years . Tip Toe unites their themes to complete a sort of trilogy, combining the anxieties of LGBTQ people, intrafamilial alienation, economic strife, the social-media panopticon, and an overarching sense of doom into a fire sermon against our toxic present. That it shares its Manchester setting with the far breezier, Y2K-era Queer as Folk underlines just how much that community’s outlook has changed in a quarter-century. And the fact that Cumming’s phenomenal performance is airing concurrently in the U.S. with The Traitors: New Blood , which he hosts with high-camp aplomb and an androgynous glam wardrobe, highlights the cognitive dissonance of a society where queerness is embraced—by everyone except the sizable faction that actively hates it. More than just Leo’s antagonist, Clive is an avatar for straight masculinity in crisis, desperately vulnerable but too terrified of showing emotion to say so. Morrissey captures that tightness of that bind. Devalued at home and work, he dabbles in conspiracy theories and marinates in videos of “real deaths.” His story can feel like an adult Adolescence .
Tip Toe also calls to mind other recent series ( BEEF , too many reality shows about feuding neighbors) and films ( Eddington , Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri ) that translate current political and social fault lines into tête-à-tête conflicts. On both sides of the Atlantic, storytellers are trying to understand the hateful tenor of the contemporary public sphere by distilling it down to its simplest, me-against-you form. The difference here is that, although Leo and other characters are shown to have healthy senses of humor, Tip Toe itself doesn’t share those titles’ tone of black-comic absurdity. It isn’t a funny show. Sometimes its seriousness veers into stridency. I didn’t find the abrupt escalation to Leo’s death particularly convincing.
Yet, as in It’s a Sin and Years & Years , it’s the incandescent clarity of Davies’ anger and fear that make Tip Toe powerful. For all the dumbed-down dialogue we get from streamers worried they’ll lose distracted viewers unless someone on screen recaps the plot every five minutes, it’s rare to hear characters plainly state things like: “History tells us one thing—that blood and fire and retribution always happen. And right now it’s coming for us.” When Stephanie confesses her worry that she’ll die in 30 years without living to see the pendulum of progress swing society out of what she calls a “new Dark Age,” I suspect she’s speaking for a lot of people. Too often in fiction (which this is, despite ending title cards that purport to update us on the characters’ lives post-Leo), social commentary is inoculated with optimism or couched in irony. In its unblinking earnestness, Tip Toe ’s melodrama accesses a truth that transcends any shortcomings of its plot.

articles.title_orig: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.title_zh: The 1893 World's Fair Is the Subject of a New 'Chicago Stories' Documentary
articles.content_orig:
“This fair not only changed Chicago, it shaped the American imagination,” says Peter Marks, one of the producers and writers of the new documentary The World’s Fair of 1893 , which leads off a new season of our Chicago Stories on Friday, October 2 at 8:00 pm and at wttw.com/chicagostories . Walt Disney’s father was a carpenter who helped build the fair, while the illustrations of the Emerald City in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, who attended, look “an awful lot like the White City” of the fair. The World’s Columbian Exposition not only inspired people; it also showed the world a new Chicago and introduced Vienna Beef, the zipper, and much more.
We spoke to Marks, his fellow producer and writer Tania Lindsay, and digital producer Meredith Francis about the fair, the documentary, and the companion website.
The Guide: Why is this World’s Fair so important to Chicago?
Peter Marks: This is the moment Chicago announced itself to the world. Only 20 years after the Great Fire , Chicago had transformed into an economic powerhouse and the birthplace of the skyscraper. [The skyscraper is the subject of another new Chicago Stories .] But people, especially New Yorkers, still dismissed us as a smelly ‘cow town.’ When Chicago beat out New York for the right to host the World’s Fair, Daniel Burnham and John Root had less than three years to turn a swamp in Jackson Park into a city that would dazzle and delight the world. Twenty-seven million visitors later, nobody could call Chicago a cow town anymore.
Tania Lindsay: It put the city on the map as a rival to New York and Paris. It also physically reshaped the city and seeded institutions, ideas, and products we still use daily.
The Guide: Why revisit the World’s Fair now?
Lindsay: Partly because there is no bad time to revisit the wonder that was the White City. And partly to remind Chicago of something about itself: That this is a city with a long history of doing hard and wonderful things, if imperfectly, and showing the world that we are much more than whatever the news says in any given year. The imperfect part matters too, and while we celebrate all the glorious wonders of the fair, the film doesn’t skip the hard parts, like who got left out, who got taken advantage of – or worse – and who carried on despite tragedy.
Marks: I think there’s something valuable about remembering a moment when Chicago took on the impossible. The fair is a reminder of Chicago’s “I Will” spirit, and what we can accomplish when we think big.
The Guide: How did you try to take a new approach towards a topic many Chicagoans already know?
Marks: One of the things we wanted to do was separate H.H. Holmes the murderer from H.H. Holmes the myth. Many people have read The Devil in the White City , in which Holmes builds this elaborate murder castle to lure unsuspecting victims. But that isn’t quite what happened. Newspaper reporters exaggerated the details, publishing fabricated diagrams of secret chambers and a crematory.
Meredith Francis: Another darker story to come out of the fair was the assassination of Chicago's mayor, Carter Harrison, just a couple days before the fair was set to close.
The Guide: What is something new that you learned in making this documentary?
Lindsay: Brownies can be highly controversial. While Bertha Palmer’s kitchen at the Palmer House Hotel is given credit as inventor of the beloved brownie, others question whether that apricot-glazed confection should be considered a brownie at all. It’s a highly sensitive topic. Some historians refused to comment, others cautiously avoided picking a side. Some said one thing off the record, and something different on. We may never know the right answer. But we’ll always have brownies.
The Guide: What’s something that most Chicagoans don’t know about the fair?
Marks: Most Chicagoans think the World’s Fair vanished, but it didn’t. If you walk down the Midway Plaisance at the University of Chicago, that’s where belly dancers once strutted and the first Ferris wheel spun. The Museum of Science and Industry was originally the Palace of Fine Arts. The Art Institute was created for the fair. There’s a ticket booth tucked in the yard of a private residence. The Obama Presidential Library rises on ground where the Horticulture and Women’s Building once stood. The fair is still very much around us if you know where to look.
Francis: On the companion website, we want people to be able to immerse themselves in this world, and to be able to imagine what it might have been like to attend the fair. We have some amazing historical images that go beyond the typical picture people might have in their heads. Our talented graphics team has created a really cool 3D imagining of what it would have been like to walk through the fair. It gives you a sense of just how expansive it was, and what it took to achieve that.
The Guide: What’s your favorite lasting impact of the fair?
Marks: For me, it’s Daniel Burnham’s vision. The White City helped inspire the City Beautiful movement and Burnham’s 1909 Plan of Chicago . There are times our skyline, parks, and museums still take my breath away.
Francis: There are a couple things that I would argue have made my life better: An early model of the modern dishwasher (invented by a woman!), and the brownie.
Lindsay: My favorite may well be the Ferris Wheel. I love that it exists because Chicago had a serious case of envy and wanted to top Paris’s 1889 World’s Fair stunner, the Eiffel Tower. George Ferris engineered the first-of-its-kind, giant wheel, with riding cars the size of city buses. It was a sensation when it debuted on the Midway Plaisance, which helped become the blueprint for the modern amusement park . Every time I see the wheel at Navy Pier, I see part of the Fair’s legacy, still spinning today.

articles.title_orig: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.title_zh: New Preliminary Real-World VEOZAH™ (fezolinetant) Data Highlights Improvements in Menopause-Related Symptoms and Sleep Outcomes
articles.content_orig:
NORTHBROOK, Ill. , Oct 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Astellas Pharma U.S., Inc. (Head of US Commercial: Mike Petroutsas, "Astellas") presented a new preliminary analysis from the Phase 4 OPTION-VMS real-world study of non-hormonal therapies (non-HTs) for bothersome vasomotor symptoms (VMS, also known as hot flashes and night sweats) at the 2026 International Menopause Society (IMS) 20 th World Congress on Menopause. The analysis showed that VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45mg) treatment was associated with statistically significant improvements from baseline in bothersome VMS at week 12, the study's primary endpoint, and improvements were observed as early as week 4. 1 VEOZAH is approved in the U.S. for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.
Statistically significant improvements were also seen across patient-reported† and objective (obtained with a medical grade wearable) sleep measures for the first time at weeks 4, 8 and 12, including a mean reduction of 2.6 nighttime awakenings from baseline at week 12. 1
Sleep disturbances are among the most commonly reported and bothersome symptoms during menopause, affecting an estimated 40–60% of menopausal women. Women with moderate to severe hot flashes are almost three times more likely to report frequent nighttime awakenings compared with women without hot flashes. 2
OPTION-VMS is a Phase 4 real-world study of women prescribed non-hormonal therapies (fezolinetant, SSRIs/SNRIs* and other non-HTs e.g. gabapentin, oxybutynin) for bothersome VMS and other menopause-associated symptoms in routine clinical practice. 1 By combining women's reported sleep experiences with objective, wearable-derived actigraphy sleep data, OPTION-VMS provides new preliminary real-world insights into sleep outcomes in routine clinical practice. The study was not designed to assess differences between treatment groups.

No new safety signals were seen with fezolinetant. Hepatic laboratory findings were mild and infrequent (2 cases of non-serious mildly elevated liver tests), none of which led to treatment or study discontinuation. 1
Prof. Marla Shapiro, C.M., Department of Family and Community Medicine, University of Toronto, Canada, and lead author of the OPTION-VMS oral presentation , commented: "Hot flashes and night sweats can have a far-reaching impact on women's daily lives, including their sleep, quality of life and overall well-being. These preliminary real-world findings add to the growing body of evidence from OPTION-VMS, demonstrating improvements in bothersome vasomotor symptoms and sleep outcomes among women treated with fezolinetant. Taken together with the broader study findings, these data contribute to a more complete understanding of women's experiences in routine clinical practice and may help inform discussions between women and their healthcare providers."
These preliminary real-world findings reinforce data from the VEOZAH clinical trial program and are complemented by interim data from the ongoing GRACE real-world study in Germany and the ongoing ADELE-AU, real world study in Australia, also being presented at the International Menopause Society (IMS) 2026. 3,4
Additional data presented at IMS 2026 provide supporting pre-clinical, clinical and real-world evidence across different study settings and geographies. 5,6,7,8,9
Shayna Mancuso, D.O., FACOG, Executive Medical Director and Head, U.S. Medical Affairs, Women's Health, Astellas "These preliminary real-world findings provide valuable insights into outcomes observed with fezolinetant (VEOZAH), including sleep quality, among women experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats. By evaluating women's experiences in routine clinical practice, we are building a deeper understanding of the outcomes that matter most to women and their clinicians."
Fezolinetant is a non-hormonal, selective neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist specifically designed to block neurokinin B binding on kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin neurons, which are involved in regulating the brain's temperature control center. By targeting this pathway, fezolinetant helps reduce the frequency and severity of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. 10,11 It is currently approved in 50 countries.
† Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Sleep Disturbance – Short Form 8b
* Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)/Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)
About OPTION-VMS OPTION-VMS (NCT06049797) is a Phase IV, longitudinal, observational, study of women aged 40-75 years with confirmed menopausal hot flashes and night sweats (also known as vasomotor symptoms or VMS) who were prescribed a non-hormonal therapy for the treatment of bothersome hot flashes and nights sweats by their healthcare provider in a real-world setting. 1 The primary objective of the study was to check if the hot flashes and night sweats that bother women change after 12 weeks (3 months) of treatment from baseline; additional outcomes include sleep quality, menopause-related quality of life, sexual health, mood, work productivity and safety.
About ADELE ADELE is an ongoing real-world observational study of women in Australia over the age of 40 who are being treated with fezolinetant for moderate to severe hot flashes and night sweats, with sleep disturbances. 4 The primary objective of the study is to evaluate improvements in real-world sleep disturbances after 12 weeks of treatment. Additional objectives include better understanding of treatment satisfaction and adherence, and treatment impacts on menopause-related quality of life (QoL) and adverse events.
About GRACE GRACE (NCT07455812) is an ongoing 24-week real-world observational study of women in Germany who have menopausal hot flashes and night sweats and have been prescribed fezolinetant. 3 The primary goal of this study is to learn about the effectiveness and safety of fezolinetant through patient surveys conducted before participants' first dose, assessed through validated patient-reported measures, including symptom improvement, menopause-related quality of life, sleep disturbance, treatment satisfaction and safety, with follow-up surveys taking place 1 week, 12 weeks and 24 weeks after their first dose.
About VEOZAH TM (fezolinetant 45 mg) VEOZAH (fezolinetant 45 mg) is a selective neurokinin 3 receptor (NK3R) antagonist, currently approved in 50 countries for the treatment of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause. Fezolinetant works by blocking neurokinin B (NKB) binding on the kisspeptin/neurokinin/dynorphin (KNDy) neuron, to modulate neuronal activity in the brain's temperature control center helping restore the balance in the brain's temperature control center (the hypothalamus) to reduce the number and intensity of hot flashes and night sweats due to menopause. 10,11

We provide transformative therapies in disease areas that include oncology, ophthalmology, urology, immunology, and women's health. Through our research and development programs, we are pioneering new healthcare solutions for diseases with high unmet medical needs. Learn more at www.astellas.com .

articles.title_orig: Material World: Quilt Fiesta Santa Fe showcases traditional and art quilts as it celebrates creativity and community
articles.title_zh: Material World: Quilt Fiesta Santa Fe showcases traditional and art quilts as it celebrates creativity and community
articles.content_orig:
As many Santa Fe artists can attest, inspiration can come from almost anything and anywhere. For Janet Avery, her creative spark came from her late father’s “hang-around” pants, a retired clergy’s stoles, a Vera place mat, and even a silk jacket worn to welcome President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton to Anchorage in 1996.
The common denominator? Fabrics of significance. For Avery, scraps of fabric bound together with thread, intention, and imagination comprises an artistic medium known as “art quilts.” They are more about original artistic expression and less about the traditional quilt’s functionality and therefore are hung on walls rather than stretched across a bed.
Among the artist’s more than 300 quilts, she has stitched works commemorating Amarillo’s Cadillac Ranch and her twin granddaughters’ births as well as serious themes, like the mass shooting in Uvalde, Texas. She’s also sewn self- portraits, using upcycled clothing scraps featured as a quilting challenge for a show in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico.
Avery chooses to focus on smaller, intricate art pieces but says the art form is as varied as the creators. “There are a gazillion talented quilters, and all are artists in their own way,” she says, and they all make deliberate choices about color, pattern, and composition.
Although she’s sewn traditional quilts, including a king-sized commissioned piece, Avery prefers making smaller art quilts.
“I get bored easily and making blocks of the same thing over and over until you get enough for a big quilt, well, I have issues. I much prefer instant gratification. I won’t do another king-sized quilt, so don’t ask,” she says with a laugh.
A centuries-old craft, quilting sits at the intersection of art, domestic labor, cultural history, and storytelling. Historically, quilting was associated with women as homemakers, sewing them to keep families warm using whatever materials they could find — old clothing, uniforms, feed and flour sacks, curtains, worn wool blankets — often designing the quilts as a family or historical narrative.
Quilting also was a social endeavor, as women gathered to sew and swap stories. The communal and social facets of quilting are still a fundamental aspect of the art form.
In fact, these artists will be in the spotlight on Friday and Saturday, October 2 and 3, during Quilt Fiesta Santa Fe, when members of the Northern New Mexico Quilt Guild host its biennial showcase that will include traditional and art quilts.
The guild’s Quilt Fiesta, which began almost 20 years ago, is a testament to the commitment and creativity of local quilters. The event includes judged categories, quilts for sale, vendor exhibits, quilting products, and a whole lot of quilt talk. The event is the guild’s primary fundraiser, and entry fees support the organization’s many service projects that include providing quilts honoring service men and women and for children and adults facing illness, loss, homelessness, and life’s hardest moments.
Art quilts by Janet Avery include Guadalupe on the Hill Rain, Lilies , Feather Flowers , and Art in the Garden . A centuries-old craft, quilting sits at the intersection of art, domestic labor, cultural history, and storytelling.
“Not only does the Quilt Fiesta create funding for these projects for the next two years, but it also shows the community what quilting is,” says Kristin Roybal, the guild’s vice president. “These quilts represent many hours of work, and we do enjoy showing what we’ve worked on. It’s nice to have your quilt hung up and celebrated.”
As an artistic community, she says, Santa Fe welcomes quilting just as it does other art forms, and the Fiesta provides an opportunity to show the many diverse techniques, themes, and innovations in the craft.
“It’s nice to show something else people are doing artistically,” Roybal says. “Society at large is going to ready-to-wear fashion and buying everything at stores. But to see that people put time and work into creating quilts, you understand it’s not a faceless machine. There’s a person behind it.”
Roybal has been quilting for 18 years and remembers her grandmother quilting. Her grandmother gave hand-stitched quilts to all her children and grandchildren. Gifting quilts continues to be a longstanding tradition.
“I like having something to put my efforts into and then gift it,” she says. “I always tell people they are to be used. If this thing is destroyed in five years because it’s been washed and used, that’s wonderful!”
Guild member Margaret Marti also grew up watching both of her grandmothers quilt, and she began sewing almost before she could walk. She says her first quilt was made from kettle cloth, a 50/50 cotton/polyester blend popular in the late 1960s through the 1970s known for its durability, wrinkle resistance, and wearing “like iron.”
“It was my first quilt, and I didn’t know to look for cotton,” Marti says. “Archaeologists will find that quilt.”
Marti says she appreciates quilting as art, although she primarily does traditional quilting rather than art quilts. “Definitely all are artful, and every quilt has a lot of soul,” she says. “It’s my art form. Or as close as I’ll ever get to having an art form.”
A quilt by Janet Avery titled ‘Feather Flowers’.
A key component to the Quilt Fiesta is seeing how others use materials and new techniques. The exhibit is as much of a show-and-tell as it is an opportunity for extended study and a quest for knowledge and education.
“I always find new things that I’ve never seen before,” Roybal says. “Seeing all of these quilts with some being so insanely complex and artistic, it’s inspiring.”
Guild members will display and compete with their quilts as a certified quilt judge critiques and evaluates quilts in a variety of categories based on design, appearance, workmanship, and construction.
Marti notes that in many instances, the Santa Fe quilters are not as interested in winning prizes as they are for the knowledge, education, and feedback they receive from the judge and the chance to chat with other quilters and newbies about their hobby.
“There’s a fair amount of pride involved,” she says. “We like people to see our work.”
Materials for today’s quilts can include batiks, silks, scarves, ties, bead embellishments, and upcycled clothing. The extensive selection of textiles, designs, and techniques brings endless possibilities, Roybal says.
“You can make it as easy or as complex as you want to,” she says. “I always suggest new quilters start small and then get into different patterns and techniques.”
She says the process at the beginning is “all ideas and fun.” And then midway into the quilting scene, she says quilters begin to ask, “‘What did I get into?’ But then it feels good to see it as a completed work, and you kind of forget some of the challenges.”
A quilt by Janet Avery titled ‘Art in the Garden’.
The Northern New Mexico Quilt Guild also has “mini” groups that focus on different techniques members are working on. And it’s these mini groups where members sew together, share tips, and new methods, and, of course, talk about what’s going on in their lives. Sometimes a guild member will bring their current quilt, and everyone will work on it together.
And as much as things change, they more stay the same — at least among quilters. ￼
Cathy Cochran-Lewis is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe. She writes about food, travel, arts, culture, and the people and places of New Mexico.

articles.title_orig: NASA Plans To Build A Permanent Base On The Moon
articles.title_zh: NASA Plans To Build A Permanent Base On The Moon
articles.content_orig:
NASA has unveiled a $20 billion initiative to build a permanent base on the Moon. Called "Ignition," it aims to test whether humans can sustainably live beyond Earth. The plan, announced on March 24, 2026, marks a major shift from short lunar visits to a long-term human presence on the Moon.
The base will be built near the lunar south pole in three phases. NASA chose the area because scientists believe water ice is trapped inside some of the regionâs permanently shadowed craters. The area also has places that receive sunlight for long periods. This could help provide power for a future base.
The first phase will run from 2026 through 2029. It will focus on launching robotic missions to the lunar south pole . These uncrewed flights will deliver rovers and scientific instruments to the Moon. The robots will explore the area and help scientists identify good locations for the base. The missions will test new systems and help NASA learn how to operate on the Moon.
The second phase will run from 2029 through 2032. During this time, NASA will begin building the infrastructure needed for longer missions. This will include early power systems, cargo and communications systems, and initial living spaces. International partners will play a major role during this phase. For example, Japanâs space agency, JAXA, is developing a pressurized rover. The vehicle will allow astronauts to live and work inside it while traveling long distances across the lunar surface.
The third and final phase will begin in 2032. It will focus on establishing a permanent lunar outpost where astronauts can live and work for extended periods. NASA will add larger habitats , communications equipment , and transportation systems.  A nuclear power plant will also be built to provide steady energy during the long lunar nights.
"The moon base will help NASA learn how to live away from Earth, and possibly later to Mars and other planets," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

articles.title_orig: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.title_zh: A rosary in the Vatican for ‘peace for all the children in the world'
articles.content_orig:
While one million children around the world offered up the Rosary for peace, about 1,300 of those voices were coming from the Vatican Gardens on the first day of the month dedicated to the RosaryâOctober 1. Children from parishes and schools around Rome gathered at the Grotto of Lourdes with Pope Leo XIV to kick off the Aid to the Church in Need initiative âOne Million Children Praying the Rosaryâ.
Representing the global dimension of this initiative, each of the five decades was recited in a different language: Italian, Spanish, Urdu, German, and Arabic.
This rosary starts a weeklong initiative drawing attention to âthe wounds and hopes of peoplesâ globallyâthe children of Ukraine and all the victims of war; families in Lebanon, Syria, and the Holy Land; persecuted Christians in Pakistan and around the world; reconciliation in South Sudan; and families in Cuba and Venezuela.
Before reciting the Marian prayer, Cardinal Kurt Koch, Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, explained that this initiative is an invitation for children to discover that âtogether with Mary, they can bring the sufferings of the world to Jesus.â
âIt is precisely the voices of the youngest, who entrust themselves to him with confidence, that find a special welcome in the heart of God,â he stressed. Throughout the weekâOctober 1-7âcommunities around the world, separated by language and distance, will be united in their prayer for peace.
âAs we contemplate the risen Christ, we ask that fear and hatred may not have the final word,â Cardinal Koch said.
In his message, Pope Leo XIV stressed the importance of this initiative and his joy at being present with the children, parents, and priests.
Encouraging the children, the Pope reminded them that they are asking Jesus and Mary for âa special gift: peace for all the children of the world, especially those who live in places where there is war, in so many countries around the world.â
He described the rosary as a âsimple prayer that everyone can prayâ and called the flowers the children had offered at the beginning of each decade as a sign of love.
The Pope urged them to think about Jesus at the important moments of his life, âwhen he brought light and peace to many people.â These included Jesusâ baptism in the Jordan, turning water in wine at the wedding of Cana, proclaiming the Kingdom of God, his Transfiguration, and when he instituted the Eucharist in the Upper Room.
Pope Leo urged the children never to forget and be thankful for these moments when Jesus âgave us wonderful giftsâ and to âask him with confidence, all united: Give us peaceâ.
Concluding his message to the children and families, the Pope highlighted how those present in the Vatican Gardens throughout this week (October 1-7) are not the only ones praying. About one million voices are joining them in this prayer.
âThink about itâ, Pope Leo stressed: âFifty million âHail Marysâ rising to Heaven from every part of the world and in every language, asking for peace, joining together like one enormous Rosary, embracing all the continents, peoples, and nations of the world.â
By praying the rosary together at the Grotto of Lourdes, he reminded everyone present that they are committing themselves to behaving well wherever they are: at home, school, in catechism class, with their parents, and when they play.
âPrayers must also be accompanied by good deeds and acts of love,â Pope Leo explained. âThat is how peace grows.â
